label: Leakage currents
lesson:
# Leakage currents

An off transistor still conducts. Subthreshold current, gate tunneling, junction leakage, band-to-band tunneling and gate-induced drain leakage add up to a static power that can rival switching power in idle blocks. Leakage drives threshold-flavor choice, power gating, standby modes and corner selection. Power analysis tools read it from Liberty tables that compact models produce, so a tool designer should know what each component is and what it depends on.

## The leakage components

Four mechanisms dominate an off MOSFET.

Subthreshold leakage flows through the channel, by diffusion over the source barrier, and scales as $10^{-V_t/S}$. It usually dominates in logic, especially for low-threshold devices at high temperature.

Gate leakage is direct tunneling through the dielectric. It fell sharply with high-k dielectrics, which allow a thicker physical layer at the same capacitance.

Junction leakage is reverse-bias current of the source and drain junctions: diffusion and generation currents, plus band-to-band tunneling where steep, heavily doped junctions (such as halo regions) create high fields.

Gate-induced drain leakage (GIDL) arises when the gate is low and the drain high: the strong field in the gate-drain overlap bends the bands enough for band-to-band tunneling, and current flows from drain to body. It grows at negative $V_{GS}$, which limits how far an off device can be pushed below threshold.

## What leakage depends on

Temperature: subthreshold leakage rises steeply as threshold falls and swing grows with temperature; a factor of several between 25 °C and 85 °C is common. Gate tunneling is nearly temperature independent.

Circuit state: two off transistors in series leak much less than one. The intermediate node rises slightly, giving the upper device negative $V_{GS}$, a body-effect threshold increase and reduced DIBL. This stack effect makes cell leakage depend on input state.

Body bias: reverse body bias raises threshold and cuts subthreshold leakage, but increases the junction field, so band-to-band and GIDL leakage rise. Beyond some bias, total leakage increases again.

Mitigation at the design level uses higher-threshold cells off the critical path, power gating with high-threshold header or footer switches that disconnect idle blocks, and retention schemes for state. Clock gating removes dynamic power but not leakage.

## How EDA models leakage

Liberty files give each cell a leakage power value per input state, because the inputs decide which transistors are off and whether they form stacks. Power tools weight these states by signal probabilities from simulation or propagation to estimate average leakage.

Leakage varies by an order of magnitude or more across process corners and temperature, so leakage numbers are only meaningful with their corner. A fast corner at high temperature is the worst-case leakage corner, while the same corner is the best case for delay.

Leakage also couples to temperature. Leakage heats the die and heat raises leakage. If leakage power rises faster with temperature than the package can remove heat, the loop runs away. Thermal-aware power analysis iterates temperature and leakage to a fixed point, and packaging decisions depend on the slope of that loop. For a tool designer this is a classic coupled nonlinear problem solved by fixed-point iteration.

## Going deeper

Roy, Mukhopadhyay and Mahmoodi-Meimand, "Leakage current mechanisms and leakage reduction techniques in deep-submicrometer CMOS circuits", Proceedings of the IEEE (2003); Rabaey, "Low Power Design Essentials" (2009).

B) Punch-through

C) Direct gate tunneling

D) Gate-induced drain leakage (GIDL)

problems.e: The large gate-to-drain field bends the bands in the drain overlap until electrons tunnel from valence to conduction band. The current flows from drain to body.

B) Electromigration current

C) Reverse-bias diode leakage of wells

A) Subthreshold leakage

B) Gate-induced drain leakage

C) Junction leakage

A) Velocity saturation: carriers slow down

B) The Miller effect: capacitance doubles

A) Which transistors are off, and whether they form stacks, depends on the inputs

B) Liberty requires it for timing arcs only

C) Input state changes the supply voltage

D) Leakage depends only on cell area
problems.a: Which transistors are off, and whether they form stacks, depends on the inputs

A device engineer lowers gate leakage by switching from SiO$_2$ to HfO$_2$ at the same EOT. Why does gate leakage fall?

A) The high-k layer is physically thicker for the same capacitance, and tunneling falls exponentially with thickness

B) HfO$_2$ has a larger band gap than SiO$_2$

C) The gate voltage is lower

D) HfO$_2$ has zero defects
problems.a: The high-k layer is physically thicker for the same capacitance, and tunneling falls exponentially with thickness
problems.e: Capacitance depends on $\varepsilon/t$, tunneling on $e^{-2\kappa t}$. A higher $\varepsilon$ permits a larger $t$. HfO$_2$ actually has a smaller gap and barrier than SiO$_2$; thickness wins.

problems.q:
Leakage heats a die, and heat raises leakage. What failure can this loop cause?

A) Latch-up, which is a purely electrical effect

B) Hold violations at low temperature

C) Gate oxide thickening

D) Thermal runaway, if leakage power grows faster with temperature than the package can remove heat
problems.a: Thermal runaway, if leakage power grows faster with temperature than the package can remove heat
problems.e: Positive electrothermal feedback is stable only while the slope of leakage power with temperature stays below the package's heat-removal slope.

label: DIBL threshold shift
lesson:
# DIBL threshold shift

Drain-induced barrier lowering is the short-channel effect that makes a transistor's threshold depend on its own drain voltage. It is quoted for every process in millivolts per volt, it is one of the first parameters a compact-model extraction fits, and it directly multiplies off-current at the supply voltage. Computing its size and its leakage cost turns the qualitative short-channel story into numbers a power tool uses.

## Threshold at high drain bias

In a short channel, the drain's field reaches the source end of the channel and lowers the potential barrier that electrons must cross. The gate then needs less voltage to turn the device on. To first order the threshold falls linearly with drain voltage:
$$V_t(V_{DS}) = V_{t,lin} - \eta\,(V_{DS} - V_{DS,lin}),$$
where $\eta$ is the DIBL coefficient in mV/V and $V_{t,lin}$ is measured at a small drain voltage, typically 50 mV.

Example: $V_{t,lin} = 0.38$ V at 0.05 V, $\eta = 80$ mV/V. At $V_{DS} = 0.85$ V, $V_t = 0.38 - 0.080 \times 0.80 = 0.316$ V.

Well-controlled FinFETs and nanosheets reach DIBL of a few tens of mV/V; late planar bulk devices at minimum length were often near or above 100 mV/V. Because the saturation threshold is what governs both off-current and drive current at the supply, DIBL feeds both speed and leakage.

## Extracting the DIBL coefficient

Extraction measures threshold twice, once in the linear regime at small $V_{DS}$ and once in saturation at $V_{DS} = V_{DD}$, using the same threshold definition (often constant current). Then
$$\eta = \frac{V_{t,lin} - V_{t,sat}}{V_{DD} - V_{DS,lin}}.$$

Example: $V_{t,lin} = 0.350$ V at 0.05 V and $V_{t,sat} = 0.290$ V at 0.75 V. $\eta = 60\ \text{mV}/0.70\ \text{V} = 85.7$ mV/V.

The value depends on the threshold definition and on length: it grows steeply as $L$ approaches the natural length. A compact model must reproduce DIBL across the length range with parameters that scale smoothly, and an extraction agent that fits only one length will produce a model that predicts the wrong leakage elsewhere. In BSIM-family models, DIBL parameters are among those fitted against short-channel devices at high drain bias.

## The leakage cost of DIBL

Off-current is exponential in threshold, so the DIBL shift multiplies leakage by
$$\frac{I_{off}(V_{DD})}{I_{off}\text{ at the low-}V_{DS}\text{ threshold}} = 10^{\eta\,\Delta V_{DS}/S}.$$

Example: $\eta = 80$ mV/V, $\Delta V_{DS} = 0.8$ V and $S = 75$ mV/decade. The threshold drop is 64 mV, which is 0.853 decades: a factor of 7.1 in off-current.

This is why DIBL appears on every process comparison table next to subthreshold swing: together they set how much threshold a device needs for a given leakage budget. It also explains why DIBL matters to timing: drive current rises with $V_{DS}$ through the same barrier lowering, so the current delivered during a transition depends on the output voltage. A model that gets DIBL right only at $V_{DS} = V_{DD}$ will mispredict the shape of the output transition.

## Going deeper

Taur and Ning, "Fundamentals of Modern VLSI Devices" (2nd ed.), section 3.2; the BSIM4 and BSIM-CMG technical manuals, sections on short-channel and DIBL parameters.

label: Threshold roll-off and the natural length
prereqs: The MOS capacitor and oxide capacitance
lesson:
# Threshold roll-off and the natural length

Threshold roll-off is the drop in threshold as channel length shrinks. Its size is governed by an electrostatic natural length set by the device's geometry, and the threshold reduction decays roughly exponentially in $L/\lambda$. This scale length is the cleanest way to compare planar, SOI, double-gate and gate-all-around devices, and to see why device architecture, not only lithography, decides how short a gate can be.

## The exponential roll-off model

Solving Poisson's equation in the channel region shows that the potential disturbance from the source and drain decays into the channel with a characteristic length $\lambda$. The threshold reduction then behaves approximately as
$$\Delta V_t(L) \approx A\, e^{-L/(2\lambda)},$$
where $A$ depends on the junction potentials and bias, and is of order the built-in potential plus a share of $V_{DS}$.

Example: $A = 1.0$ V and $\lambda = 8$ nm. At $L = 40$ nm, $\Delta V_t = e^{-2.5} = 82$ mV. At $L = 30$ nm, $e^{-1.875} = 153$ mV.

The steep exponential is the key message. Each nanometre shaved off near the roll-off knee costs more threshold than the last. That is why gate-length variation, around a nanometre, becomes significant threshold variation in short devices, and why processes choose gate lengths several natural lengths long.

## The natural length of a device

The natural length depends on how many gates surround a thin body and how thick the body and dielectric are. For a single-gate fully depleted SOI device, a standard estimate is
$$\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_{Si}}{\varepsilon_{ox}}t_{Si}t_{ox}}.$$
For a symmetric double gate it becomes $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{Si}t_{Si}t_{ox}/(2\varepsilon_{ox})}$, smaller by $\sqrt 2$, and gate-all-around geometries shrink it further.

Example: $\varepsilon_{Si}/\varepsilon_{ox} = 3$, $t_{Si} = 10$ nm and $t_{ox} = 1$ nm. Single gate: $\lambda = \sqrt{30} = 5.48$ nm. Double gate: $\lambda = \sqrt{15} = 3.87$ nm.

The lesson for device scaling is that a thinner body and more gates shrink $\lambda$ and so allow a shorter gate at the same roll-off. That is the electrostatic argument for FinFETs (thin fin, gate on three sides) and nanosheets (gate on all sides). Planar bulk devices have an effective body depth set by depletion, which doping can only reduce so far.

## Minimum gate length for a roll-off budget

Inverting the model gives the shortest gate that keeps roll-off within a budget $\Delta V_{max}$:
$$L_{min} = 2\lambda \ln\frac{A}{\Delta V_{max}}.$$

Example: $A = 1.0$ V, $\lambda = 5.5$ nm and a budget of 20 mV. $L_{min} = 11 \times \ln 50 = 43$ nm. Halving $\lambda$ halves $L_{min}$.

A common rule of thumb follows: keep $L$ at roughly five to ten natural lengths for acceptable short-channel behavior. Device architects use this budget to choose fin width, sheet thickness and EOT for a target gate pitch. For EDA, the consequence shows up in design rules and in the models: gate lengths in a library are fixed by the process, and length biasing (drawing slightly longer gates on non-critical cells) is used to trade a little speed for lower leakage, exploiting exactly the steep roll-off curve.

## Going deeper

Yan, Ourmazd and Lee, "Scaling the Si MOSFET: from bulk to SOI to bulk", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (1992); Colinge, "FinFETs and Other Multi-Gate Transistors" (2008), chapter 1.

label: Leakage across threshold-voltage flavors
lesson:
# Leakage across threshold-voltage flavors

A modern library offers the same cells in several threshold flavors: ultra-low, low, standard and high threshold. Lower threshold is faster and leakier, by a factor set by the subthreshold swing. Leakage-recovery and multi-threshold optimization in implementation tools swap flavors cell by cell, so the arithmetic of threshold steps and leakage ratios is what those tools optimize.

## Leakage ratio between flavors

Off-current scales as $10^{-V_t/S}$. Two flavors that differ by $\Delta V_t$ with everything else equal have a leakage ratio
$$\frac{I_{off,low}}{I_{off,high}} = 10^{\Delta V_t/S}.$$

Example: LVT is 80 mV below SVT and $S = 75$ mV/decade. The ratio is $10^{1.067} = 11.7$: an LVT cell leaks about twelve times as much as its SVT twin.

Drive current changes far less. In saturation it depends on overdrive to a power between 1 and 2, so 80 mV less threshold at a 0.75 V supply might add 15 to 25% current. That asymmetry, an order of magnitude in leakage for a fraction of speed, is why low-threshold cells are rationed to critical paths. Real flavors also differ slightly in DIBL and capacitance, which characterized libraries capture and simple ratios do not.

## Threshold step for a leakage target

Process and library teams often work backwards: a new flavor should cut leakage by a factor $R$. The threshold step needed is
$$\Delta V_t = S \log_{10} R.$$

Example: a factor of 10 at $S = 70$ mV/decade needs 70 mV; a factor of 30 needs $70 \times 1.477 = 103$ mV.

In high-k metal-gate processes, flavors are made mostly with different work-function metal stacks and sometimes with channel or gate-length changes, rather than doping alone. The available steps are therefore discrete and process-specific. For a power-optimization engine, the flavors are a small menu of cells with known delay and leakage tables. A leakage-recovery pass walks paths with positive slack and swaps cells to higher threshold while the slack allows, a greedy or Lagrangian optimization on exactly these trade-offs.

## Leakage of a mixed-flavor block

A block's leakage is the sum over cells. With counts $N_{LVT}$, $N_{SVT}$, $N_{HVT}$ and SVT leakage $I_0$ per cell,
$$I_{block} = I_0\left(N_{LVT}10^{\Delta_1/S} + N_{SVT} + N_{HVT}10^{-\Delta_2/S}\right).$$

Example: 5000 LVT, 40000 SVT and 30000 HVT cells, $I_0 = 1$ nA, LVT 70 mV below SVT, HVT 70 mV above, $S = 70$ mV/decade. LVT cells leak 10 nA each and HVT 0.1 nA. The total is $50 + 40 + 3 = 93$ µA. The 7% of cells that are LVT contribute over half the leakage.

This is the standard pattern: leakage concentrates in the low-threshold minority. An optimization engine therefore gets the most leakage recovery per unit of slack by targeting LVT cells first. The same formula, evaluated at each corner with corner-specific swing and leakage, is what a power report sums from Liberty data.

## Going deeper

Wei, Roy and others, "Design and optimization of dual-threshold circuits for low-voltage low-power applications", IEEE Transactions on VLSI Systems (1999); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed.), chapter on timing closure.

label: Gate tunneling leakage and high-k dielectrics
prereqs: The MOS capacitor and oxide capacitance
lesson:
# Gate tunneling leakage and high-k dielectrics

As SiO$_2$ gate dielectrics thinned toward 1.2 nm, direct tunneling current through them became a significant part of standby power. High-k dielectrics solved this by making the layer physically thicker at the same capacitance. Computing physical thickness, tunneling reduction and chip-level gate current shows why the change was worth new materials and new compact-model terms, and why gate leakage still appears in leakage reports.

## Physical thickness at a given EOT

Capacitance depends on $\varepsilon/t$, so a dielectric with relative permittivity $k$ reaches the capacitance of SiO$_2$ of thickness EOT at a physical thickness
$$t_{hk} = \text{EOT}\cdot\frac{k}{3.9}.$$

Example: EOT $= 0.9$ nm with HfO$_2$-like $k = 20$ needs $t_{hk} = 0.9 \times 20/3.9 = 4.6$ nm, about five times thicker than the equivalent SiO$_2$.

In practice the stack includes a thin SiO$_2$-like interfacial layer, often a few tenths of a nanometre, which uses up part of the EOT budget at low permittivity. The high-k layer must then supply the rest. High-k materials also bring problems a device engineer must manage: more interface and bulk traps (which feed PBTI), remote phonon scattering that lowers mobility, and threshold shifts from charge and dipoles at the interfaces, which is part of why metal gates and work-function engineering arrived together with high-k.

## How much leakage high-k saves

Direct tunneling scales as $e^{-2\kappa t}$, and $\kappa$ depends on the barrier height and tunneling mass. High-k dielectrics have lower barriers than SiO$_2$ (HfO$_2$ around 1.5 eV versus about 3.1 eV for electrons), so $\kappa$ is smaller, but the thickness gain dominates.

Example with equal prefactors: SiO$_2$ at 1.0 nm with $\kappa = 6.4$ nm$^{-1}$ gives an exponent of 12.8. A $k = 20$ layer at the same EOT is 5.13 nm thick; with $\kappa = 3.0$ nm$^{-1}$ its exponent is 30.8. The difference, 18.0, is $18.0/2.303 = 7.8$ decades.

This estimate is crude: prefactors, interfacial layers and image-force barrier lowering all matter. But it captures why the industry accepted a materials change: orders of magnitude of gate leakage at the same capacitance. Compact gate-current models keep the exponential thickness dependence, with parameters fitted to measured gate current per area.

## Gate leakage of a whole chip

Gate current scales with gate area, so chip-level gate leakage is current density times total biased gate area:
$$I_g = J_g \cdot N \cdot \overline{W L}.$$

Example: $10^9$ transistors with average gate area $0.1 \times 0.02$ µm$^2$ give $2 \times 10^6$ µm$^2$ $= 0.02$ cm$^2$. At $J_g = 1$ A/cm$^2$, the chip draws 20 mA of gate current, a large standby budget for a mobile chip.

Two details matter for a power tool. Gate leakage flows only where the gate is biased relative to the channel or source and drain, so it depends on logic state, as subthreshold leakage does. And it is nearly independent of temperature, unlike subthreshold leakage, so its share of total leakage is largest at cold corners. Liberty leakage values include it through characterization, but separating the components is what lets a designer reason about which mitigation (power gating, flavor swaps, voltage reduction) will help.

## Going deeper

Wilk, Wallace and Anthony, "High-k gate dielectrics: current status and materials properties considerations", Journal of Applied Physics (2001); Robertson, Reports on Progress in Physics (2006).

label: Silicon on insulator
prereqs: Threshold roll-off and the natural length
lesson:
# Silicon on insulator

Silicon on insulator builds transistors in a thin silicon film on a buried oxide instead of in a bulk wafer. The insulator removes most junction capacitance and the latch-up path, and in fully depleted SOI it gives a thin body with good electrostatics and a usable back gate. SOI also brings its own modeling problems, floating bodies and self-heating, that compact models and characterization flows must handle.

## Partially and fully depleted SOI

In partially depleted SOI (PD-SOI), the silicon film is thicker than the maximum depletion depth under the gate. A neutral body region remains, and unless it is tied to a contact it floats. Charge from impact ionization and junction leakage collects there and shifts the body potential, and through the body effect the threshold. Delays then depend on switching history (the history effect), and output characteristics can show a kink.

In fully depleted SOI (FD-SOI), the film is thin enough, a few nanometres to around ten, that the gate depletes it completely. There is no neutral body to float. The thin film limits how far the drain field can reach, giving good short-channel control without heavy channel doping, which also reduces random dopant fluctuation.

In both, the buried oxide removes most bottom-wall junction capacitance and breaks the well-substrate thyristor, so latch-up largely disappears.

## Back-gate bias

In FD-SOI with a thin buried oxide, the substrate under the oxide acts as a second gate. Biasing it shifts the threshold with a coupling coefficient $r$, often quoted in mV per volt of back bias:
$$V_t = V_{t0} - r\,V_{BB} \quad \text{(NMOS, forward back bias positive)}.$$

Example: $V_{t0} = 380$ mV and $r = 80$ mV/V. A forward back bias of 1.0 V gives $V_t = 300$ mV; a reverse bias of 1.0 V gives 460 mV.

This is a far stronger knob than bulk body bias, because it couples through a thin oxide rather than through depletion charge, and it works over a wider voltage range since there are no forward-biased junctions to limit it. Designs use it adaptively: forward bias to speed up slow dies or high-performance modes, reverse bias to cut leakage in standby.

## What SOI means for models and flows

Compact models for PD-SOI (such as BSIM-SOI) carry an internal body node with slow charge and discharge time constants, so transient simulations must run long enough for the body state to settle, and timing can depend on activity history.

The buried oxide conducts heat roughly a hundred times worse than silicon, so SOI devices self-heat: the channel runs hotter than the ambient under sustained current, lowering mobility. SOI models include a thermal node with a thermal resistance and capacitance.

FD-SOI back biasing changes threshold, speed and leakage after fabrication, so libraries are characterized at several back-bias points, and implementation tools must sign off timing and power at each operating point the chip will use. Models with independent front and back gates (BSIM-IMG) exist for exactly this. Finally, thin films bring film-thickness variation and quantum confinement into threshold, which statistical models must capture.

## Going deeper

Colinge, "Silicon-on-Insulator Technology: Materials to VLSI" (3rd ed.); the BSIM-SOI and BSIM-IMG technical manuals.

label: FinFETs
prereqs: Threshold roll-off and the natural length
lesson:
# FinFETs

A FinFET wraps the gate around a thin vertical fin of silicon, controlling the channel from both sidewalls and the top. The thin fin gives strong electrostatic control, lowering subthreshold swing and DIBL, and the vertical sidewalls give more channel width per unit of layout area. For EDA the most visible consequence is that transistor width became an integer number of fins, which reshaped standard cells, sizing and the compact models behind them.

## Effective width of a FinFET

Current flows along the fin's surfaces under the gate: two sidewalls of height $H_{fin}$ and the top of width $W_{fin}$. The effective electrical width of one fin is approximately
$$W_{fin,eff} = 2H_{fin} + W_{fin},$$
and a device with $N$ fins has $W_{eff} = N(2H_{fin} + W_{fin})$.

Example: fins 45 nm tall and 7 nm wide give 97 nm per fin. Three fins give $W_{eff} = 291$ nm.

Because the fins are tall and closely spaced, the effective width per unit of footprint can exceed what a planar device of the same footprint offers. The fin width is kept small, several nanometres, so that the body is fully depleted and the gate controls it from both sides. The fin is typically undoped or lightly doped, with threshold set mostly by the gate work-function metal, which reduces random dopant fluctuation.

## Drive current from effective width

Processes quote drive current per unit of effective width or per unit of footprint; the two differ, so the convention matters. With current per effective width $I'$,
$$I_{on} = W_{eff}\cdot I'.$$

Example: 3 fins of 97 nm effective width each (291 nm $= 0.291$ µm) at $I' = 900$ µA/µm give $I_{on} = 262$ µA.

Electrostatically, the double-gate-like control gives subthreshold swings near 65 to 70 mV/decade and DIBL of a few tens of mV/V, much better than late planar bulk. This let FinFET processes lower threshold and supply voltage while keeping leakage acceptable. On the other hand, fins add parasitics: gate-to-contact capacitance between closely spaced fins and gates, and series resistance in the narrow source and drain regions. In many FinFET cells these parasitics, not the intrinsic channel, dominate delay, which is why middle-of-line extraction became critical.

## Width quantization

A FinFET's width comes only in whole fins. A device that needs current $I$ when each fin delivers $I_{fin}$ uses
$$N = \lceil I / I_{fin} \rceil$$
fins, and overshoots the requirement.

Example: 25 µA per fin and a requirement of 140 µA gives $\lceil 5.6 \rceil = 6$ fins, delivering 150 µA.

Quantization reshaped design. Standard-cell drive strengths map to fin counts, and cell height is set in fin pitches (track heights). Analog designers lost fine width control and use fin count and finger count instead, with matching depending on identical fin arrays. Sizing algorithms in synthesis and optimization operate on discrete cell sizes anyway, but custom circuits and SRAM bitcells, where ratios between transistors matter, must work with integer ratios such as 1:1:2 fins. Compact models such as BSIM-CMG take fin count, fin height and fin width as instance parameters.

## Going deeper

Hisamoto and others, "FinFET: a self-aligned double-gate MOSFET scalable to 20 nm", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (2000); Colinge, "FinFETs and Other Multi-Gate Transistors" (2008); the BSIM-CMG technical manual.

label: Gate-all-around nanosheet transistors
lesson:
# Gate-all-around nanosheet transistors

Gate-all-around nanosheet transistors stack several thin horizontal silicon sheets and wrap the gate completely around each one. Surrounding the channel on all sides gives better electrostatic control than a FinFET's three sides, and the sheet width is a continuous layout choice, which undoes the width quantization that fins imposed. Nanosheets are the device architecture that follows FinFETs at leading-edge logic nodes.

## Effective width of a nanosheet stack

Each sheet of width $W$ and thickness $T$ conducts along its full perimeter, since the gate surrounds it. The effective width of a stack of $N$ sheets is
$$W_{eff} = N \cdot 2(W + T).$$

Example: 3 sheets, each 30 nm wide and 6 nm thick, give $W_{eff} = 3 \times 72 = 216$ nm.

Sheet thickness is kept to a few nanometres so that the gate controls the whole cross-section, and sheets are separated vertically by the gate stack itself. The fabrication sequence grows alternating silicon and silicon-germanium layers, patterns them, then removes the SiGe sacrificial layers to release the sheets before depositing the gate around them. Inner spacers between the sheets isolate the gate from the source and drain, and their quality matters for parasitic capacitance.

## Nanosheet versus FinFET in one footprint

For a fixed cell footprint, the comparison is effective width per footprint and electrostatic control. A FinFET adds width by adding fins side by side; a nanosheet adds width by stacking sheets vertically and widening them.

Example: two fins of height 50 nm and width 6 nm give $2 \times 106 = 212$ nm. Three sheets of width 35 nm and thickness 5 nm give $3 \times 80 = 240$ nm, a ratio of 1.13, with the gate wrapping every surface.

The ratio depends heavily on sheet width and count, so it can go either way. The real gains are better electrostatics (lower swing and DIBL at the same gate length, enabling shorter gates or lower supply) and design flexibility. Costs include more complex fabrication, higher parasitic capacitance between sheets and gate, and new variability sources such as sheet thickness and sheet-to-sheet differences.

## Continuous width as a design knob

Unlike fin count, sheet width can be drawn at any value within design rules. To reach a target effective width with $N$ sheets of thickness $T$,
$$W = \frac{W_{eff}}{2N} - T.$$

Example: a target of 200 nm with 3 sheets of 5 nm gives $W = 200/6 - 5 = 28.3$ nm.

This flexibility returns a knob that FinFETs took away. Standard-cell libraries can offer sheet widths tuned per cell, and SRAM designers can set pull-up, pull-down and pass-gate strengths with non-integer ratios. It also makes the device model's width dependence matter again: compact models for gate-all-around devices (BSIM-CMG supports GAA geometries) take sheet width, thickness and count as instance parameters, and extraction must fit across widths. Very narrow and very wide sheets behave differently, the former through stronger edge effects and the latter through weaker electrostatics at sheet edges.

## Going deeper

Loubet and others, "Stacked nanosheet gate-all-around transistor to enable scaling beyond FinFET", Symposium on VLSI Technology (2017); the BSIM-CMG technical manual, gate-all-around sections.

label: Quantum confinement in thin bodies
lesson:
# Quantum confinement in thin bodies

When a channel is only a few nanometres thick, electrons behave as waves trapped in a box: their allowed energies split into subbands, and the lowest one sits above the bulk band edge. This quantum confinement raises the threshold, moves the charge away from the interface and makes threshold sensitive to body thickness. Every thin-body device, from FD-SOI to nanosheets, needs a compact model that captures it.

## Ground-state confinement energy

Model the thin body as an infinite square well of width $t$. The allowed energies above the band edge are
$$E_n = \frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m^*t^2}, \qquad n = 1, 2, \ldots$$
Using $\hbar^2/(2m_0) = 0.0381$ eV nm$^2$, $E_1 = 0.376/((m^*/m_0)\,t^2)$ eV with $t$ in nm.

Example: $t = 5$ nm and confinement mass $0.916\,m_0$ (silicon's heavy longitudinal mass, relevant for one valley pair on a (100) surface) give $E_1 = 0.376/(0.916 \times 25) = 16.4$ meV. With $m^* = 0.19\,m_0$, $E_1 = 79$ meV.

The infinite well overestimates the energy somewhat, since real barriers are finite and fields tilt the well. Still, the scaling, $E_1 \propto 1/(m^* t^2)$, is correct and is what matters for design: halving the body thickness quadruples the confinement energy.

## Subband spacing

The second level of the well sits at $E_2 = 4E_1$, so the spacing between the first two subbands is
$$E_2 - E_1 = 3E_1.$$

Example: $t = 5$ nm with $m^* = 0.19\,m_0$ gives $E_1 = 79$ meV and a spacing of 237 meV, about nine times $kT$ at room temperature. Almost all electrons then occupy the lowest subband (or lowest few, counting silicon's several valleys with different masses).

When the spacing is many $kT$, transport is effectively two-dimensional, and the valley with the lightest confinement mass in the transport direction may not be the lowest in energy. This changes effective mobility and density of states. Strong confinement also redistributes electrons among silicon's conduction valleys, which is one way crystal orientation and strain affect thin-body mobility. Device simulators handle this with Schrödinger-Poisson solvers or density-gradient corrections, and compact models fold it into effective parameters.

## Threshold and band-gap effects

Confinement raises the lowest electron state and lowers the highest hole state, so the effective band gap widens by
$$\Delta E_g = E_{1,e} + E_{1,h}.$$

Example: a 4 nm body with electron mass $0.916\,m_0$ and hole mass $0.29\,m_0$. $E_{1,e} = 0.376/(0.916 \times 16) = 25.7$ meV and $E_{1,h} = 0.376/(0.29 \times 16) = 81.0$ meV, a widening of 107 meV.

For a transistor the electron shift raises the threshold by roughly $E_{1,e}/q$, and because $E_1 \propto 1/t^2$, threshold depends on body thickness: $dE_1/dt = -2E_1/t$. At $t = 4$ nm with $E_1 = 25.7$ meV, a 0.5 nm thickness variation shifts it by about 6 meV, and much more for lighter masses or thinner bodies. Confinement also pushes the charge centroid away from the interface, adding to effective oxide thickness. Compact models for FinFETs and nanosheets include both effects.

## Going deeper

Davies, "The Physics of Low-Dimensional Semiconductors" (1998), chapter 4; Omura and others, "Quantum-mechanical effects on the threshold voltage of ultrathin-SOI nMOSFETs", IEEE Electron Device Letters (1993).

label: CFET and the stacking outlook
prereqs: CMOS as a complementary device pair
lesson:
# CFET and the stacking outlook

A complementary FET stacks the NMOS and PMOS of a CMOS pair vertically instead of placing them side by side. Built from gate-all-around nanosheets, it removes the lateral n-to-p separation that sets standard-cell height, promising a large density step. It is still an outlook rather than a production technology, and its implications for layout, extraction, routing and modeling are what an EDA tool designer should anticipate.

## What a CFET stacks

In planar, FinFET and nanosheet CMOS, the n-type and p-type devices sit in separate regions of the cell, separated by spacing that sets part of the cell height. A CFET places a nanosheet stack of one polarity directly on top of a stack of the other, sharing one footprint. A common gate can wrap both, and the output node connects the top and bottom drains through a vertical contact.

Two fabrication approaches are discussed. Monolithic integration builds both tiers in one wafer flow, patterning the stacked layers together. Sequential integration builds the bottom tier, bonds a second silicon layer on top and then builds the upper tier, which eases alignment and lets each tier be optimized but limits the thermal budget of the upper-tier steps.

CFET is not new channel physics: each tier is a gate-all-around device. Its novelty is three-dimensional arrangement of the CMOS pair, which pushes complexity into contacts, interconnect and process integration.

## Layout, routing and extraction

Removing the n-to-p separation shrinks cell height, which reduces the number of horizontal routing tracks over each cell. Pin access gets harder, so placement and detailed routing must treat pin access as a first-class constraint.

Power delivery competes for the same scarce front-side tracks. Backside power delivery, where supply rails are routed on the back of the thinned wafer and connected to the devices from below, frees front-side tracks and gives the bottom tier a short supply path, so CFET and backside power are often discussed together.

Extraction must represent tier-aware geometry: which tier each contact and gate segment is on, vertical contacts between tiers, and capacitive coupling between stacked devices and their local interconnect, within nanometres vertically. LVS and DRC decks need tier-aware layers. Cell layout generators and place-and-route data models that assume a planar device layer need extensions for which tier a pin lives on.

## Outlook and modeling

For compact modeling, each tier is a nanosheet device, so gate-all-around channel models largely carry over. The new work is in tier-to-tier electrostatic and capacitive coupling, separate parameters for each tier (the tiers may see different thermal budgets and so different thresholds and mobility), and the parasitic network of vertical contacts.

Thermal behavior is a concern: stacking raises power per footprint and buries one tier farther from the heat-removal path, so self-heating terms and thermal-aware analysis matter more.

Density claims should be read with care. The gain from removing n-to-p spacing is real, but the net cell size depends on contact schemes, vertical interconnect and track count, and production results are not yet established. For a tool designer the safe assumption is that CFET will stress the same places FinFETs and nanosheets did, namely parasitics, pin access and variability, and add genuinely three-dimensional geometry to tools that were built around a single device layer.

## Going deeper

Ryckaert and others, "The complementary FET (CFET) for CMOS scaling beyond N3", Symposium on VLSI Technology (2018); the IEEE International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS), More Moore chapter.

label: Sources of device variability
lesson:
# Sources of device variability

No two transistors are identical. Dopant atoms land at random, gate edges are rough, metal grains differ, and process conditions drift across a wafer. Where variability comes from decides how it must be modeled: as a global shift shared by a whole die, as independent per-device randomness, or as a deterministic function of layout. Statistical timing, Monte Carlo simulation and SRAM yield analysis each depend on getting that classification right.

## Atomistic sources of mismatch

Three physical mechanisms dominate random device-to-device variation in modern transistors.

Random dopant fluctuation (RDF): a small doped channel contains only tens to hundreds of dopant atoms. Their number follows Poisson statistics and their positions are random, so the depletion charge and threshold vary. RDF grows as devices shrink and as channel doping rises.

Line-edge roughness (LER): lithography and etch leave gate edges that wander by a nanometre or so. The local gate length varies along the width, and through short-channel effects that becomes threshold and current variation. Fin-edge roughness plays the same role for fin width.

Metal gate granularity (MGG): the work-function metal forms grains of different crystal orientations, each with its own work function. The effective work function over a small channel depends on which grains sit above it.

Undoped thin-body devices (FinFETs, nanosheets, FD-SOI) largely suppressed RDF, leaving geometry and work-function variation as the main random terms.

## Global, local and systematic variation

Variation is classified by how it correlates.

Global (die-to-die, wafer-to-wafer, lot-to-lot) variation shifts every device on a die together: a slightly thicker oxide or different anneal for the whole wafer. It preserves matching between neighbors and is what process corners describe.

Local (within-die, random) variation is independent from device to device, even for identical neighbors. RDF, LER and MGG are local. It is what Pelgrom mismatch and LVF sigmas describe.

Systematic variation is deterministic given the layout or position: lithographic proximity effects, stress from nearby wells and shallow-trench isolation, pattern-density effects of etch and polish, and smooth gradients across a wafer. Layout-dependent effects (LDEs) are modeled with extra instance parameters such as distance to well edge or diffusion length, which extraction computes from the layout.

A Monte Carlo SPICE run must sample global parameters once per die and local parameters per device instance; mixing these up either destroys or hides matching.

## Why classification matters downstream

Different classes propagate differently through a design.

Along a path of $N$ gates, independent local deviations add in quadrature, so the path's sigma grows as $\sqrt N$ while its mean grows as $N$. The relative variation falls as $1/\sqrt N$. Global variation is fully correlated and adds linearly. Statistical timing methods (AOCV, POCV with LVF) build these rules in, and treating correlated variation as independent understates risk.

Circuits that depend on matching are dominated by local variation in the far tail. A 6T SRAM cell's read stability depends on the strength ratio of transistors inside one cell, and a large array needs that ratio to hold out to around 5 or 6 sigma. Sense amplifiers and comparators have offset set by input-pair mismatch.

Systematic effects are the most fixable: once a layout-dependent effect is modeled, it can be predicted, compensated in design, or removed by layout rules. That is why extraction tools carry LDE parameters into the netlist.

## Going deeper

Asenov, "Random dopant induced threshold voltage lowering and fluctuations in sub-0.1 µm MOSFETs", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (1998); Kuhn and others, "Process technology variation", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (2011).

lesson:
# Pelgrom mismatch scaling

Pelgrom's law says that random threshold mismatch between two identical, adjacent transistors shrinks as the square root of their gate area. It is the single most used variability formula in circuit design and the basis of the local-variation parameters in statistical compact models. Analog sizing, SRAM design and the area cost of precision all follow from it.

## Mismatch scales with area

Random local variation averages over the gate area. If each small patch of channel contributes an independent random threshold deviation, the average over area $WL$ has a standard deviation proportional to $1/\sqrt{WL}$. For the threshold difference between two adjacent identical devices,
$$\sigma_{\Delta V_t} = \frac{A_{V_t}}{\sqrt{WL}},$$
where the Pelgrom coefficient $A_{V_t}$ is in mV µm and is a property of the process.

Example: $A_{V_t} = 2$ mV µm, $W = 0.5$ µm, $L = 0.1$ µm. $WL = 0.05$ µm$^2$, so $\sigma_{\Delta V_t} = 2/0.2236 = 8.94$ mV.

The coefficient has fallen with oxide thickness over the generations, since thinner oxide reduces the threshold impact of a given charge fluctuation, and FinFETs reduced it further by removing channel dopants. A distance term for gradients exists in Pelgrom's original paper, but for neighbors the area term dominates.

## Area needed for a matching target

Inverting the law gives the gate area required for a mismatch target:
$$WL = \left(\frac{A_{V_t}}{\sigma_{target}}\right)^2.$$

Example: a comparator needs $\sigma_{\Delta V_t} \le 1$ mV with $A_{V_t} = 2.5$ mV µm. $WL = 6.25$ µm$^2$, more than a hundred times a minimum logic device.

The quadratic cost is the precision-area trade-off of analog design: halving mismatch costs four times the area, and four times the capacitance, which slows the circuit and costs power. This is why offset calibration, chopping and digital correction exist. For an EDA flow, it means device sizes in analog blocks are set by statistics rather than by drive current, and a layout tool must preserve matching by symmetric, interdigitated or common-centroid placement, because gradients add systematic mismatch that Pelgrom's random term does not include.

## From pair mismatch to single-device sigma

Pelgrom's coefficient describes the difference between two devices. If each device's local deviation is independent with sigma $\sigma_{V_t}$, the difference has variance $2\sigma_{V_t}^2$, so
$$\sigma_{V_t} = \frac{\sigma_{\Delta V_t}}{\sqrt 2}.$$
Statistical compact models specify the single-device local sigma, so this conversion matters when comparing a datasheet's mismatch number with a model card.

Example: $A_{V_t} = 1.5$ mV µm and a minimum device of $0.05 \times 0.02$ µm$^2$. $\sigma_{\Delta V_t} = 1.5/\sqrt{0.001} = 47.4$ mV, so $\sigma_{V_t} = 33.5$ mV and $3\sigma = 101$ mV, a large fraction of a 300 mV threshold.

For small devices this is enormous, and for an SRAM array with millions of cells the relevant tail is 5 to 6 sigma. That is why SRAM bitcells, built from near-minimum devices, are the most variability-limited circuits on a chip, and why SRAM yield analysis needs rare-event statistics rather than plain Monte Carlo.

## Going deeper

Pelgrom, Duinmaijer and Welbers, "Matching properties of MOS transistors", IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits (1989); Kinget, "Device mismatch and tradeoffs in the design of analog circuits", IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits (2005).

label: Process corners and statistical device models
lesson:
# Process corners and statistical device models

A process corner is a single set of model parameters representing a deliberately extreme process, such as slow NMOS with slow PMOS. Corners are how most timing signoff still handles global variation, while statistical models and Monte Carlo handle the rest. Knowing what corners represent, how independent sources combine, and where corner methods are pessimistic or blind is essential for anyone writing a timer or a characterization flow.

## What corners represent

Foundries ship corner model cards named by NMOS and PMOS speed: TT (typical), SS, FF, and the skewed corners SF (slow NMOS, fast PMOS) and FS. Each is a global shift of device parameters, typically placed at a few sigma of the die-to-die distribution. A signoff corner combines a process corner with a supply voltage and temperature (PVT), plus interconnect corners for parasitics.

Skewed corners matter for circuits whose function depends on n-to-p strength ratios: SRAM write and read margins, level shifters, and ratioed logic.

Temperature does not monotonically slow devices. Mobility falls with temperature, slowing them, but threshold also falls, speeding them. At low supply voltage, where overdrive is small, the threshold effect can dominate, so delay decreases with temperature: temperature inversion. The slow corner at low voltage may then be the cold one, which is why signoff covers both temperature extremes.

## Combining independent sigmas

When independent Gaussian sources affect one parameter, their variances add:
$$\sigma_{total} = \sqrt{\sigma_{global}^2 + \sigma_{local}^2}.$$

Example: a threshold with nominal 400 mV, global sigma 20 mV and local sigma 15 mV. $\sigma_{total} = 25$ mV, so the $+3\sigma$ point for one device on a random die is 475 mV. Adding the sigmas linearly would give 505 mV, treating the sources as fully correlated and overstating the extreme.

The same arithmetic explains why corners are pessimistic for paths. A corner shifts global parameters to $3\sigma$; stacking worst-case local variation on every gate of a path at the same time adds a second set of correlated extremes that rarely co-occur. Statistical timing separates the two: corners for global variation, LVF-based POCV for local variation, with local sigmas combined in quadrature along the path.

## Statistical models and Monte Carlo

A statistical compact model carries distributions for selected parameters (threshold, mobility, effective length, oxide thickness), split into global and local parts with their correlations. Monte Carlo SPICE samples them to estimate the distribution of a circuit metric.

Library characterization uses Monte Carlo per arc, slew and load to produce LVF tables of delay sigma due to local variation. Analog designers use it to estimate offsets and yields.

Plain Monte Carlo has a sampling limit. A 6-sigma event has probability around $10^{-9}$, so a thousand samples with no failure say almost nothing beyond about 3 sigma. Rare-event methods (importance sampling, statistical blockade, scaled-sigma sampling and others) concentrate samples near the failure region, and SRAM yield analysis relies on them.

For a tool designer, Monte Carlo is also a cost problem: thousands of SPICE runs per cell arc. Surrogate models and sensitivity-based methods that predict sigma from a few runs are an active way to cut it.

## Going deeper

Orshansky, Nassif and Boning, "Design for Manufacturability and Statistical Design" (2008); the Liberty Variation Format (LVF) documentation in the Liberty reference manual.

A timing signoff uses SS at low voltage and high or low temperature. Why can either temperature be worst for delay?

A) Delay always rises with temperature

B) Low temperature always speeds wires only

C) Temperature inversion: at low supply, the falling threshold can outweigh falling mobility as temperature rises

D) Temperature never affects delay

problems.q:
A device's threshold has nominal value 300 mV, an independent global (die-to-die) sigma of 23 mV and a local (within-die) sigma of 23 mV. For a single device on a random die, what threshold sits at the $+2\sigma$ point of the combined distribution, in mV?

A) 392

B) 346

C) 365.1

B) 370

C) 341.2

label: Bias temperature instability and hot carriers
lesson:
# Bias temperature instability and hot carriers

Transistors age. Under bias and temperature, traps form at the gate dielectric interface and in the dielectric, and the threshold drifts upward. Bias temperature instability (BTI) happens under static gate bias; hot-carrier injection (HCI) happens while current flows at high drain voltage. Both slow circuits over years, and timing signoff must cover the end of life, not only time zero.

## Bias temperature instability

Negative bias temperature instability (NBTI) affects PMOS devices whose gate is held negative relative to the source and body, at elevated temperature. No drain current is needed: the vertical field across the dielectric and heat create interface traps and trap charge in the dielectric. The threshold magnitude rises and the drive current falls. A PMOS whose input sits low, such as a pull-up in an idle gate, is under NBTI stress.

Positive BTI (PBTI) is the NMOS counterpart under positive gate bias. It was minor with SiO$_2$ dielectrics but became significant with high-k stacks, where electrons trap in the high-k layer.

BTI partially recovers when stress is removed, as some trapped charge escapes. Measured degradation therefore depends on the delay between stress and measurement, and on the duty cycle of the stress. Aging models express degradation as a function of stress time, voltage, temperature and duty cycle, often with separate recoverable and permanent components.

## Power-law time dependence

BTI shift grows sublinearly with stress time, commonly modeled as a power law:
$$\Delta V_t = A\,t^{n},$$
with $n$ typically between about 0.1 and 0.3, and $A$ depending on voltage and temperature.

Example: a stress test shows 10 mV after 1000 hours with $n = 0.2$. At 10 years (87,600 hours) the ratio of times is 87.6, so $\Delta V_t = 10 \times 87.6^{0.2} = 24.5$ mV. Linear extrapolation in time would predict 876 mV, absurdly wrong.

A power law with a small exponent means most degradation happens early, and that extrapolation over many decades of time magnifies any error in the exponent. Changing $n$ from 0.2 to 0.25 changes the 10-year prediction to 30.6 mV. Reliability engineers fit $n$ from stress data measured over several decades of time, at accelerated voltage and temperature, and then extrapolate both in time and in stress conditions.

## Hot-carrier injection

Hot-carrier injection needs current and a high lateral field together. Carriers accelerated through the high field near the drain gain enough energy to create interface traps or to be injected into the gate dielectric. Damage concentrates near the drain end of the channel, where the field peaks, which makes it asymmetric: a device degraded in forward operation behaves differently when source and drain are swapped.

HCI damage accumulates per switching event, so it is driven by activity: clock buffers and output drivers that switch often at full supply age most. Idle gates suffer BTI but little HCI.

Historically HCI was worse at low temperature, because reduced phonon scattering lets carriers reach higher energies, while BTI is thermally activated and worse when hot. In advanced FinFET and nanosheet devices the picture is more complex, with self-heating raising channel temperature and multiple-carrier mechanisms at low voltage. Aging-aware flows therefore need both activity (for HCI) and static signal probabilities (for BTI) per device.

## Going deeper

Schroder and Babcock, "Negative bias temperature instability: road to cross in deep submicron silicon semiconductor manufacturing", Journal of Applied Physics (2003); Grasser (ed.), "Bias Temperature Instability for Devices and Circuits" (2014).

problems.q:
Why does BTI recover partially when the stress is removed?

A) Part of the trapped charge is released when the field is removed

B) Recovery is a measurement artifact only

C) The gate oxide regrows

D) Dopants diffuse back into the channel
problems.a: Part of the trapped charge is released when the field is removed
problems.e: Some traps empty on relaxation, so measured degradation depends on the delay between stress and measurement. Duty-cycle-aware models capture this.

problems.q:
Which BTI variant became significant for NMOS with high-k metal-gate stacks?

A) Electromigration

B) Positive bias temperature instability (PBTI)

C) Hot-hole injection

D) Negative BTI in NMOS
problems.a: Positive bias temperature instability (PBTI)
problems.e: With high-k dielectrics, electron trapping in the high-k layer under positive gate bias gives an NMOS threshold shift.

problems.q:
What happens to a transistor's threshold and drive current under BTI stress?

A) The gate capacitance doubles

B) The threshold magnitude rises and the drive current falls

C) The threshold falls and current rises

D) Both are unchanged; only leakage rises
problems.a: The threshold magnitude rises and the drive current falls
problems.e: Interface and oxide traps capture charge that opposes the gate. $|V_t|$ rises, the overdrive shrinks and the device slows.

B) 27.2

C) 8.7

D) 148

label: Time-dependent dielectric breakdown
prereqs: Gate tunneling leakage and high-k dielectrics
lesson:
# Time-dependent dielectric breakdown

Time-dependent dielectric breakdown is the wear-out of a gate dielectric under sustained field: defects accumulate until a conducting path forms and the gate shorts. Breakdown times are statistical and follow a Weibull distribution, and a chip fails at its weakest gate, so a chip's lifetime depends on its total gate area. Reliability limits on supply voltage, and overdrive limits in design rules, come from these statistics.

## The Weibull failure distribution

Breakdown times of nominally identical capacitors follow a Weibull distribution:
$$F(t) = 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta}\right],$$
where $F$ is the cumulative fraction failed, $\eta$ is the characteristic life (the time at which 63.2% have failed) and $\beta$ is the shape parameter. Thin dielectrics have small $\beta$, often near 1 to 2, meaning a wide spread.

Example: $\eta = 100$ years and $\beta = 1.5$. At 10 years, $(0.1)^{1.5} = 0.0316$ and $F = 1 - e^{-0.0316} = 3.1\%$.

Plotting $\ln(-\ln(1 - F))$ against $\ln t$ gives a straight line of slope $\beta$, the Weibull plot reliability engineers use to fit data. The Weibull form arises naturally from weakest-link statistics: a dielectric fails when its first percolation path completes, which is the minimum of many independent local failure times.

## Time to a target failure fraction

Products are specified at low failure fractions, such as 0.01% or 0.1%, not at 63%. Inverting the Weibull distribution,
$$t_F = \eta\left[-\ln(1 - F)\right]^{1/\beta}.$$
For small $F$, $-\ln(1 - F) \approx F$.

Example: $\eta = 100$ years, $\beta = 1.5$, $F = 0.1\%$. $t_F = 100 \times (0.0010005)^{1/1.5} = 100 \times 0.01001 = 1.0$ year.

The low-percentile lifetime is far below $\eta$, and the smaller $\beta$ is, the further below. That is the danger of thin dielectrics: their wide distributions push early failures much earlier for a given characteristic life. Reliability qualification therefore extracts both $\eta$ and $\beta$ carefully, since an error in $\beta$ moves the low-percentile prediction by orders of magnitude.

## Scaling from test structures to a chip

Test capacitors are small; a chip has a large total gate area. If breakdown is a weakest-link process over area, the Weibull characteristic life scales as
$$\eta_{chip} = \eta_{test}\left(\frac{A_{test}}{A_{chip}}\right)^{1/\beta},$$
with $\beta$ unchanged.

Example: test structures of $10^{-4}$ cm$^2$ with $\eta = 5000$ years at use conditions and $\beta = 1.5$. A chip with 0.1 cm$^2$ of gate area has $\eta_{chip} = 5000 \times (10^{-3})^{0.667} = 5000 \times 0.01 = 50$ years.

Area scaling is why chip reliability is worse than device reliability, and why it worsens as chips grow. With small $\beta$ the penalty is severe. For EDA, this links reliability to design: total biased gate area, the fraction of time gates are under stress, and local overvoltage (such as from ringing on I/O) all enter. Reliability signoff tools check voltage limits per device type and stress time, derived from these models.

## Going deeper

Degraeve and others, "New insights in the relation between electron trap generation and the statistical properties of oxide breakdown", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (1998); JEDEC JEP122, "Failure Mechanisms and Models for Semiconductor Devices".

problems.q: Gate-oxide breakdown times follow a Weibull distribution $F(t) = 1 - e^{-(t/\eta)^{\beta}}$ with $\eta = 140$ years and $\beta = 2.5$. What percentage of parts has failed after 5 years? Round to 4 decimal places.

Gate-oxide breakdown times follow a Weibull distribution $F(t) = 1 - e^{-(t/\eta)^{\beta}}$ with $\eta = 70$ years and $\beta = 2.5$. What percentage of parts has failed after 10 years? Round to 3 decimal places.

Gate-oxide breakdown times follow a Weibull distribution $F(t) = 1 - e^{-(t/\eta)^{\beta}}$ with $\eta = 140$ years and $\beta = 1$. What percentage of parts has failed after 4 years? Round to 2 decimal places.
Oxide breakdown follows a Weibull distribution with $\eta = 50$ years and $\beta = 2$. At what time has 1% of the population failed, in years? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Invert $F = 1 - e^{-(t/\eta)^\beta}$: $t = \eta(-\ln(1-F))^{1/\beta} = 50 \times (0.0100503)^{1/2} = 5.01$ years. Low failure fractions sit far below $\eta$.

problems.q: Oxide breakdown follows a Weibull distribution with $\eta = 110$ years and $\beta = 1.2$. At what time has 1% of the population failed, in years? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Invert $F = 1 - e^{-(t/\eta)^\beta}$: $t = \eta(-\ln(1-F))^{1/\beta} = 110 \times (0.0100503)^{1/1.2} = 2.38$ years. Low failure fractions sit far below $\eta$.

problems.q: Oxide breakdown follows a Weibull distribution with $\eta = 60$ years and $\beta = 2.5$. At what time has 0.01% of the population failed, in years? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Invert $F = 1 - e^{-(t/\eta)^\beta}$: $t = \eta(-\ln(1-F))^{1/\beta} = 60 \times (0.000100005)^{1/2.5} = 1.51$ years. Low failure fractions sit far below $\eta$.

problems.q: Test capacitors of area $10^{-5}$ cm$^2$ show Weibull oxide breakdown with characteristic life 12000 years (extrapolated to use conditions) and $\beta = 2.5$. A chip has a total gate area of 0.1 cm$^2$. Using weakest-link area scaling, what is the chip's characteristic life, in years? Round to the nearest whole number.
problems.e: Weakest-link scaling gives $\eta_{chip} = \eta_{test}(A_{test}/A_{chip})^{1/\beta} = 12000 \times (0.0001)^{1/2.5} = 301$ years. A larger area has more weak spots, and a low $\beta$ makes the penalty steeper.

problems.q: Test capacitors of area $10^{-5}$ cm$^2$ show Weibull oxide breakdown with characteristic life 9000 years (extrapolated to use conditions) and $\beta = 1.2$. A chip has a total gate area of 0.5 cm$^2$. Using weakest-link area scaling, what is the chip's characteristic life, in years? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Weakest-link scaling gives $\eta_{chip} = \eta_{test}(A_{test}/A_{chip})^{1/\beta} = 9000 \times (2 \times 10^{-5})^{1/1.2} = 1.09$ years. A larger area has more weak spots, and a low $\beta$ makes the penalty steeper.

problems.q: Test capacitors of area $10^{-4}$ cm$^2$ show Weibull oxide breakdown with characteristic life 8000 years (extrapolated to use conditions) and $\beta = 1$. A chip has a total gate area of 0.05 cm$^2$. Using weakest-link area scaling, what is the chip's characteristic life, in years? Round to 1 decimal place.
problems.e: Weakest-link scaling gives $\eta_{chip} = \eta_{test}(A_{test}/A_{chip})^{1/\beta} = 8000 \times (0.002)^{1/1} = 16$ years. A larger area has more weak spots, and a low $\beta$ makes the penalty steeper.

label: Temperature and voltage acceleration
prereqs: Bias temperature instability and hot carriers
lesson:
# Temperature and voltage acceleration

A ten-year lifetime cannot be measured before a product ships, so reliability is tested under accelerated stress: higher temperature and higher voltage compress years into weeks. Acceleration models translate stress results back to use conditions. They are the bridge between reliability experiments and the aging models and voltage limits that EDA flows enforce, and their extrapolation is a central source of risk.

## Thermal acceleration

Thermally activated mechanisms follow the Arrhenius model: the rate is proportional to $e^{-E_a/kT}$, where $E_a$ is the activation energy. The acceleration factor between a stress temperature and a use temperature (both in kelvin) is
$$AF_T = \exp\left[\frac{E_a}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{use}} - \frac{1}{T_{stress}}\right)\right].$$

Example: $E_a = 0.7$ eV, use at 85 °C (358 K), stress at 150 °C (423 K). $E_a/k = 8124$ K and $1/358 - 1/423 = 4.29 \times 10^{-4}$, so $AF_T = e^{3.49} = 32.7$.

Activation energies differ by mechanism, roughly a few tenths of an eV to about 1 eV, so a single stress test cannot be translated without knowing which mechanism dominates. Using the wrong $E_a$ misestimates lifetime exponentially. Temperature must also be the device's actual channel temperature, which self-heating can raise well above ambient in advanced devices.

## Voltage acceleration

Higher voltage raises the field across the dielectric and the energy of carriers, accelerating wear-out. Several empirical forms are used: exponential in voltage or field (the E model), exponential in inverse field (1/E model) and power law in voltage. In the exponential form,
$$t \propto e^{-\gamma V}, \qquad AF_V = e^{\gamma(V_{stress} - V_{use})}.$$

Example: $\gamma = 8$ V$^{-1}$, stress at 1.2 V and use at 0.8 V. $AF_V = e^{3.2} = 24.5$.

The models agree inside the measured range and diverge wildly when extrapolated to use voltage, which is the core difficulty: extrapolating from 1.2 V to 0.8 V with the wrong model can be off by orders of magnitude. Reliability teams choose models with physical backing for each mechanism (for thin-oxide TDDB, power-law voltage dependence is widely used) and stress at several voltages to constrain the fit.

## Lifetime at use conditions

When temperature and voltage effects are treated as independent, their factors multiply:
$$t_{use} = t_{stress}\cdot AF_T \cdot AF_V.$$

Example: a failure criterion is reached after 500 hours at 150 °C and 1.2 V. With $AF_T = 32.7$ and $AF_V = 24.5$, $t_{use} = 500 \times 32.7 \times 24.5 = 400{,}600$ hours, about 45.7 years.

Independence is itself an assumption; for some mechanisms the activation energy depends on voltage. And the result applies to the stated failure criterion and failure fraction, typically through the Weibull or log-normal statistics of the stressed population. For EDA, these extrapolated lifetimes become the operating limits encoded in reliability rules (maximum voltage per device type, allowed overdrive time, current-density limits) and the stress parameters of aging models that produce aged timing libraries.

## Going deeper

JEDEC JEP122, "Failure Mechanisms and Models for Semiconductor Devices"; McPherson, "Reliability Physics and Engineering: Time-to-Failure Modeling" (3rd ed.).

label: Aging-aware device models
prereqs: Bias temperature instability and hot carriers
Process corners and statistical device models
lesson:
# Aging-aware device models

Aging-aware design turns device degradation physics into numbers that timing and power tools can use. A reliability simulator applies BTI and HCI shifts to compact-model parameters according to each device's stress, and characterization produces aged libraries for end-of-life signoff. The modeling chain, from mission profile to aged Liberty file, is where device physics meets EDA most directly in reliability.

## From stress to aged models

An aging flow has three parts.

A mission profile describes how the product is used: supply voltages, temperatures, operating modes and their fractions of life, often over ten years.

Device stress comes from simulation or signal statistics: for BTI, the fraction of time each transistor's gate is under stress (static probability) and the recovery between stresses; for HCI, the switching activity and the drain voltage during transitions.

Aging models then compute parameter shifts per device, mostly in threshold and mobility, using fitted equations in stress time, voltage, temperature and duty cycle. Reliability-aware simulators apply these shifts to the base compact model, leaving its I-V equations unchanged, and re-simulate to see the degraded behavior. Compact-model aging extensions standardize this interface.

Characterizing standard cells with the shifted models produces aged Liberty libraries, which static timing analysis uses exactly like fresh ones.

## Timing consequences

Aging mostly slows transistors, so setup checks are usually worst with aged libraries. But aging is not uniform.

Different devices see different stress. A clock-tree branch whose buffers idle at one logic level for long periods ages differently from a branch that toggles, so clock skew drifts over life. Skew is a difference, so asymmetric aging can create new setup or hold violations that time-zero analysis never saw.

Hold checks depend on relative delays and can be worst with fresh, fast devices or when aging slows the capture clock more than the data path. Signoff therefore uses both fresh and aged views.

A single worst-case aged library assumes every cell was maximally stressed, which is safe but pessimistic. Instance-specific or activity-aware aging analysis recovers margin by aging each cell according to its own stress. The cost is a much larger characterization and analysis problem, a natural target for fast surrogate models.

## Model risks

Aging predictions rest on extrapolation in three directions: from short stress times to a decade, from high stress voltage to use voltage, and from high temperature to use temperature. A power-law exponent fitted over a few decades of time and extrapolated two more magnifies fitting error; mechanisms may also change outside the stressed window.

Recovery complicates the profile: the same total stress time gives different shifts depending on how stress and relaxation alternate. Static probability captures much of this for logic, but high-frequency switching and long idle periods behave differently.

Temperature must be the local channel temperature. FinFET and nanosheet channels self-heat because heat escapes poorly through narrow fins and sheets, so devices age as if hotter than the ambient.

Static circuits have their own failure modes: an SRAM cell storing one value for years stresses one side of its cross-coupled pair, and the growing mismatch erodes its stability margin. Adaptive voltage scaling that raises supply to compensate aging also accelerates aging, so its schedule must be checked against the models.

## Going deeper

Reddy and others, "Impact of negative bias temperature instability on digital circuit reliability", IRPS (2002); the Si2 Compact Model Coalition documentation on the open model interface for reliability (OMI) and aging.

label: Dennard scaling and its end
lesson:
# Dennard scaling and its end

In 1974 Dennard and colleagues showed that shrinking every MOSFET dimension and the supply voltage by the same factor keeps the electric field constant, makes circuits faster and keeps power density flat. For three decades this constant-field scaling, together with Moore's observation of doubling transistor counts, drove the industry. Its end, when voltage stopped scaling, is why modern chips are power-limited and why EDA tools optimize power as hard as timing.

## Constant-field scaling rules

Scale every linear dimension (length, width, oxide thickness, junction depth) and the supply voltage by $s < 1$, and increase doping by $1/s$. Then the electric field is unchanged and:
voltage and current scale by $s$;
capacitance scales by $s$ (area $s^2$ over thickness $s$);
gate delay $CV/I$ scales by $s$;
power per circuit $VI$ scales by $s^2$;
area per circuit scales by $s^2$;
power density stays constant;
switching energy $CV^2$ scales by $s^3$.

Example: $s = 0.7$ for one generation. Delay becomes 0.7 of its old value, power per circuit 0.49, energy per switch 0.343, while power density is unchanged.

The constant field kept reliability (oxide stress, hot carriers) under control. Every generation delivered faster, cheaper, lower-energy circuits at no cost in heat per area, which is why it was such a powerful engine.

## Moore's law and density

Moore's observation (1965, revised in 1975) was that the number of components per chip at minimum cost was doubling at a regular interval, which settled near two years. Constant-field scaling supplied the means: shrinking linear dimensions by 0.7 per generation multiplies density by $1/0.49 = 2.04$.

Transistor count grows as
$$N(t) = N_0 \cdot 2^{t/T}.$$
Example: 2 billion transistors with $T = 2$ years gives $2 \times 2^{3} = 16$ billion after 6 years.

Moore's law is an economic and industrial observation, not a physical law, and the doubling period has varied. Density growth continued after Dennard scaling ended, through FinFETs, nanosheets, design-technology co-optimization (smaller cells from fewer tracks, buried or backside power rails) and multi-die packaging. But the benefits per transistor changed: density kept growing while speed and energy per operation improved far more slowly.

## Why Dennard scaling ended

Constant-field scaling requires the threshold voltage to scale with the supply. But off-current depends on $V_t$ through the subthreshold swing, which is fixed at no better than about 60 mV/decade at room temperature. Lowering $V_t$ by 60 to 70 mV costs roughly ten times more leakage. Around the mid-2000s, with $V_{DD}$ near 1 V, further threshold reduction would have made leakage unacceptable, so supply voltage stopped scaling.

With $V_{DD}$ fixed, capacitance per gate scaling by $s$ and frequency rising by $1/s$, the power per gate $CV^2f$ stays constant while density rises by $1/s^2$. Power density then grows by about $2\times$ per generation, so clock frequency plateaued instead.

Example: two generations at $s = 0.7$ with fixed voltage: power density $\times (1/0.49)^2 = 4.2$.

The result was the power wall: multicore designs, aggressive clock and power gating, multiple threshold flavors, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, and power as a first-class objective in synthesis, placement and timing optimization.

## Going deeper

Dennard and others, "Design of ion-implanted MOSFET's with very small physical dimensions", IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits (1974); Moore, "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits", Electronics (1965); Bohr, "A 30 year retrospective on Dennard's MOSFET scaling paper", IEEE SSCS Newsletter (2007).

label: Generalized scaling and the power wall
lesson:
# Generalized scaling and the power wall

Generalized scaling separates the shrink factor of dimensions from that of voltage. It lets a device or architecture engineer ask what happens when voltage scales more slowly than geometry, the situation after Dennard scaling ended. The resulting factors for delay and power density quantify the power wall, and they are the back-of-the-envelope models behind DVFS policies and power-performance trade-offs.

## Generalized delay scaling

Shrink all dimensions, including oxide thickness, by $1/\kappa$, and the supply voltage by $1/s$, with $1 \le s \le \kappa$. Using the long-channel current $I \propto (W/L)C_{ox}V^2$:
$W/L$ is unchanged, $C_{ox}$ rises by $\kappa$, so current scales by $\kappa/s^2$;
gate capacitance $\propto WL/t_{ox}$ scales by $1/\kappa$;
delay $CV/I$ scales by $(1/\kappa)(1/s)/(\kappa/s^2) = s/\kappa^2$.

Example: $\kappa = 1.4$ and $s = 1.1$. Delay scales by $1.1/1.96 = 0.561$, faster than Dennard's $1/\kappa = 0.714$.

With $s = \kappa$ this reduces to constant-field scaling. With $s < \kappa$ the field grows by $\kappa/s$, which gives more speed but stresses reliability. The long-channel current law is an assumption; with velocity saturation the current scales less favorably, so these factors are upper bounds on the speed benefit.

## Generalized power density

Power per device is $VI \propto (1/s)(\kappa/s^2) = \kappa/s^3$ when frequency follows the delay. Device density rises by $\kappa^2$. So power density scales by
$$\frac{\kappa^3}{s^3}.$$

Example: $\kappa = 1.4$, $s = 1.1$. Power density scales by $(1.4/1.1)^3 = 2.06$ per generation.

Only $s = \kappa$, full voltage scaling, keeps power density constant. Every bit of voltage that fails to scale costs power density cubically under these assumptions. After the threshold floor stopped voltage scaling ($s$ near 1), raising frequency with the delay would have multiplied power density by nearly $\kappa^3$ per generation, far beyond what packaging can remove. This is the quantitative content of the power wall, and why frequency stopped following device speed.

## Power density at fixed frequency

Industry responded by freezing clock frequency and spending density on more cores and wider datapaths. With frequency fixed, dynamic power per device is $CV^2f \propto (1/\kappa)(1/s^2)$, and with density $\kappa^2$:
$$\text{power density} \propto \frac{\kappa}{s^2}.$$

Example: $\kappa = 1.4$, $s = 1.1$: $1.4/1.21 = 1.16$ per generation. With no voltage scaling at all ($s = 1$), power density still grows by $\kappa$.

So even a frozen clock does not hold power flat without voltage scaling. Not every transistor can switch at full rate within the power budget, a situation sometimes described as dark silicon. The engineering responses are what EDA tools now optimize: clock gating and power gating to idle unused logic, multiple voltage domains and DVFS, near-threshold operation for efficiency, multi-threshold libraries, and power-aware synthesis and placement. Each one is a way of making $\alpha C V^2 f$ smaller where it matters.

## Going deeper

Baccarani, Wordeman and Dennard, "Generalized scaling theory and its application to a 1/4 micrometer MOSFET design", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (1984); Taur and Ning, "Fundamentals of Modern VLSI Devices" (2nd ed.), section 4.1.

label: The threshold-voltage floor
prereqs: Generalized scaling and the power wall
lesson:
# The threshold-voltage floor

The threshold voltage has a floor set by leakage: the off-current at $V_{GS} = 0$ is the current at threshold divided by ten for every swing's worth of threshold. With swing stuck near 60 to 80 mV/decade, a leakage budget fixes a minimum threshold, and with it a minimum useful supply voltage. This is the arithmetic that ended voltage scaling and that every low-power design trade-off still runs into.

## Minimum threshold for an off-current budget

Define threshold by a constant current, $I_{V_t}$ per micron at $V_{GS} = V_t$. Below threshold the current falls a decade per swing $S$, so
$$I_{off} = I_{V_t}\cdot 10^{-V_t/S} \quad\Rightarrow\quad V_t \ge S\log_{10}\frac{I_{V_t}}{I_{off,max}}.$$

Example: $I_{V_t} = 300$ nA/µm, a budget of 100 pA/µm and $S = 75$ mV/decade. The ratio is 3000, so $V_t \ge 75 \times 3.477 = 261$ mV.

Each decade of leakage budget costs one swing of threshold. A high-performance device with a loose budget might sit near 200 mV; a low-power mobile device with a strict budget near 400 mV or more. With supply around three to four thresholds for reasonable overdrive and noise margins, the floor on $V_t$ becomes a floor on $V_{DD}$. Steeper-swing devices (tunnel FETs, negative-capacitance FETs) are research attempts to break this floor.

## The hot corner sets the floor

Swing is proportional to absolute temperature for a fixed slope factor: $S(T) = S_{300}\cdot T/300$. Leakage budgets must hold at the hottest operating temperature, where swing is worst and threshold is also lower.

Example: $S_{300} = 70$ mV/decade, $I_{V_t} = 200$ nA/µm and a budget of 50 pA/µm. At 300 K, $V_t \ge 70 \times \log_{10}4000 = 252$ mV. At 398 K (125 °C) the swing is 92.9 mV/decade and the floor rises to 335 mV. This simple version ignores the drop of threshold with temperature itself, which raises the requirement further.

So the threshold must be set for hot silicon, but delay often matters most at the slow corner, which at low voltage may be cold because of temperature inversion. That tension, leakage set hot, speed set by whichever corner is slowest, is why multi-corner multi-mode signoff exists and why threshold flavor choice is corner-dependent.

## The on-off ratio

The ratio of on-current to off-current measures how good a switch a transistor is. With $I_{off} = I_{V_t}10^{-V_t/S}$,
$$\log_{10}\frac{I_{on}}{I_{off}} = \log_{10}\frac{I_{on}}{I_{V_t}} + \frac{V_t}{S}.$$

Example: $I_{on} = 1000$ µA/µm, $I_{V_t} = 0.3$ µA/µm, $V_t = 300$ mV and $S = 75$ mV/decade. The ratio is $\log_{10}(3333) + 4 = 7.52$ decades.

Logic needs several decades of on-off ratio so that millions of idle devices do not swamp the active ones. Raising threshold increases the off-side decades but lowers $I_{on}$ through reduced overdrive; lowering supply cuts $I_{on}$ directly. Every point on the power-performance curve that a process or library offers is a choice of these terms. Better swing, from FinFET and nanosheet electrostatics, buys extra decades at the same threshold, which processes spent on lower threshold and supply.

## Going deeper

Frank, Dennard and others, "Device scaling limits of Si MOSFETs and their application dependencies", Proceedings of the IEEE (2001); Ionescu and Riel, "Tunnel field-effect transistors as energy-efficient electronic switches", Nature (2011).
