label: TCAD device simulation
lesson:
# TCAD device simulation

Technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulates semiconductor fabrication and device behavior from physics. Process TCAD predicts structures and doping from implant, diffusion, oxidation and etch steps; device TCAD solves carrier transport in those structures to get I-V and C-V curves. TCAD is far too slow for circuits, but it is how a new device is explored, and how compact models are calibrated before silicon exists.

## Process and device simulation

Process TCAD models fabrication: ion implantation profiles, dopant diffusion and activation during anneals, oxidation, deposition and etch. Its output is a geometry with doping and material regions, the input to device simulation.

Device TCAD solves the drift-diffusion equations (or more detailed transport models) on a mesh of that structure, with physical models for mobility, recombination, tunneling and quantum corrections. Biasing the contacts and solving yields terminal currents and charges.

The mesh must be refined where quantities change over nanometres: near junctions, depletion edges and the gate-dielectric interface, where the inversion layer is about a nanometre thick. Most device simulators use a finite-volume (box) discretization with Scharfetter-Gummel fluxes along mesh edges, which conserves current exactly and remains stable for large potential steps between nodes. A 2D simulation of a planar device has thousands to tens of thousands of nodes; a 3D FinFET or nanosheet may have hundreds of thousands.

## Solving and calibrating

The discretized equations are a large sparse nonlinear system. Simulators solve them with Newton's method, either fully coupled or with Gummel-style decoupled iterations at low bias. Each Newton step needs a sparse linear solve; in 3D, fill-in makes direct factorization expensive, and iterative solvers with preconditioners are common.

Newton converges only from a good initial guess, so bias is ramped in steps, each converged solution seeding the next. A sweep of $I_D$ against $V_{GS}$ is a sequence of such continuation steps.

Small-signal capacitances come from an AC analysis that linearizes the system around a DC operating point, or from differentiating terminal charge with respect to voltage.

Calibration fits the physical model parameters, such as mobility coefficients, recombination lifetimes and doping-profile details, until simulated curves match measured silicon. A calibrated deck can then predict the effect of a change before it is fabricated, which is the purpose of TCAD in a process or design-technology loop.

## TCAD in the design flow

A single 3D TCAD bias point can take minutes; a full I-V family can take hours. A compact model evaluates in microseconds. This speed gap decides TCAD's role: it never runs inside circuit simulation. Instead it feeds compact-model extraction for new technologies, design-technology co-optimization (DTCO), and variability studies.

In DTCO, device options (fin height, sheet width, spacer thickness, contact scheme) are simulated in TCAD, turned into compact models, used to characterize standard cells and evaluated on circuit metrics such as ring-oscillator delay and power. Statistical TCAD samples random dopant positions, edge roughness or metal grains to produce variability distributions that statistical compact models must reproduce.

Commercial TCAD suites dominate industrial use. In open source, DEVSIM is a programmable finite-volume device simulator with a scripting interface, useful for learning and for research flows. For an EDA tool designer, TCAD is a slow, accurate engine at the device end of a loop whose fast engines are compact models and surrogates.

## Going deeper

Vasileska, Goodnick and Klimeck, "Computational Electronics: Semiclassical and Quantum Device Modeling and Simulation" (2010); the DEVSIM documentation; Selberherr, "Analysis and Simulation of Semiconductor Devices" (1984).

problems.q:
Which discretization do most device simulators use for the semiconductor equations on unstructured meshes?

A) Monte Carlo sampling of the potential

B) A finite-volume (box) method with Scharfetter-Gummel fluxes along edges

C) Explicit time stepping on a uniform grid only

D) Spectral methods with Fourier modes
problems.a: A finite-volume (box) method with Scharfetter-Gummel fluxes along edges
problems.e: Box integration conserves current exactly across control volumes, and Scharfetter-Gummel fluxes stay stable for large potential steps between nodes.

problems.q:

A) To calibrate and extract compact-model parameters before silicon is available, and to explore device options

B) To run static timing directly

C) To generate the layout

D) As the transistor model inside SPICE for full chips
problems.a: To calibrate and extract compact-model parameters before silicon is available, and to explore device options
problems.e: TCAD is far too slow to call inside circuit simulation. Its curves feed compact-model extraction and design-technology co-optimization.

problems.a: Potential and carrier densities change over nanometres there, and a coarse mesh gives wrong currents

label: Compact transistor models
lesson:
# Compact transistor models

A compact model is the closed-form description of a transistor that a circuit simulator evaluates at every Newton iteration for every device. It must be accurate across bias, geometry and temperature, fast, smooth, and charge conserving. Its equations and parameters are the contract between a foundry and every design team, and every timing library is characterized through it. Knowing what a compact model must capture, and why, is basic for anyone building simulators or characterization tools.

## The contract with the simulator

At each Newton iteration, SPICE asks each device model: given terminal voltages (and temperature), what are the terminal currents and charges, and their derivatives? The derivatives are the conductances $\partial I/\partial V$ and capacitances $\partial Q/\partial V$ that fill the Jacobian.

Three properties follow. Smoothness: currents and charges must be continuous with continuous derivatives across all regions (subthreshold, linear, saturation, accumulation), because a kink in $g_m$ or $g_{ds}$ makes Newton oscillate between regions; analog distortion analysis needs higher derivatives smooth too. Charge conservation: terminal charges must be defined first and capacitances derived from them; the older Meyer capacitance model was not charge conserving and could create or destroy charge in switched circuits. Speed: evaluation cost multiplies by devices, iterations and time steps.

Unlike TCAD, a compact model does not solve PDEs. It uses physics-derived closed forms with fitted parameters, which is why it can be fast enough.

## Formulations and qualification

Compact MOSFET models fall into three families by their core variable. Threshold-voltage-based models (BSIM3, BSIM4) build regional expressions around $V_t$ and blend them with smoothing functions. Surface-potential-based models (PSP, BSIM-CMG) solve for the surface potential from the gate bias and electrostatics, then derive charge and current, giving one continuous description from weak to strong inversion. Inversion-charge-based models (EKV-style) use the inversion charge as the core variable.

A model must scale with geometry: one parameter set must predict all legal widths and lengths, through built-in dependences or binning. It must include temperature, since corners span cold to hot.

Qualification checks go beyond fitting $I_D$. The Gummel symmetry test drives the device symmetrically around $V_{DS} = 0$ and checks that source-drain swap leaves the physics unchanged and higher derivatives are smooth, which passive mixers and switches require. Other checks cover $g_m/I_D$ behavior, output conductance, C-V curves and noise.

## Engineering a compact model

Model evaluation can be a large fraction of SPICE run time on post-layout netlists with millions of devices, so expressions are chosen for speed as well as accuracy.

Why not a table of measured I-V points? Tables are exact at their points, but derivatives between points depend on the interpolant, can be discontinuous, and say nothing outside the table. Physics-based expressions extrapolate sensibly, stay smooth and conserve charge.

A model is qualified over a range of bias, geometry and temperature. Outside it, the equations still evaluate but nobody has verified them, so simulators can warn on out-of-range operation.

Models also carry noise (channel thermal noise and flicker noise, both bias and geometry dependent), parasitic resistances and capacitances, gate and junction leakage, layout-dependent stress effects and, through extensions, aging. Each is a separately parameterized piece. For a tool designer, the important point is that the model is a module behind a narrow interface, which is exactly why the frontier treats it as a plug-in seam.

## Going deeper

Tsividis and McAndrew, "Operation and Modeling of the MOS Transistor" (3rd ed.); McAndrew, "Validation of MOSFET model source-drain symmetry", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (2006); Gildenblat (ed.), "Compact Modeling: Principles, Techniques and Applications" (2010).

A) SPICE cannot read tables

B) It extrapolates sensibly, stays smooth and conserves charge, while tables need interpolation that can break derivatives

C) Physics models need no parameters

D) Tables are always less accurate at measured points
problems.a: It extrapolates sensibly, stays smooth and conserves charge, while tables need interpolation that can break derivatives
problems.e: Tables are exact at their points but derivatives between points depend on the interpolant, and behaviour outside the table is undefined.

label: Single-piece I-V interpolation
lesson:
# Single-piece I-V interpolation

A compact model must describe weak inversion (exponential current) and strong inversion (square-law or velocity-limited current) with one smooth expression, so that Newton iterations never see a kink. Charge-based models do this with an interpolation function, $\ln^2(1 + e^x)$, that approaches each asymptote at the right end. Evaluating it and its limits shows concretely how a single-piece model replaces piecewise regions.

## A single-piece interpolation

EKV-style models write the forward current as
$$I_D = I_{spec}\,F(x), \qquad F(x) = \ln^2\!\left(1 + e^{x}\right), \qquad x = \frac{V_{GS} - V_t}{2n\,kT/q},$$
where $I_{spec}$ is a specific current proportional to $W/L$, mobility, oxide capacitance and $(kT/q)^2$. (The complete model also subtracts a reverse term in the drain voltage, which vanishes in saturation.)

Example: $n = 1.3$, overdrive 0 V. Then $x = 0$ and $F = (\ln 2)^2 = 0.480$. At overdrive 100 mV, $x = 0.1/(2 \times 1.3 \times 0.02585) = 1.488$, $\ln(1 + e^{1.488}) = 1.689$ and $F = 2.86$.

The function is infinitely differentiable everywhere, so the current, transconductance and all higher derivatives are continuous through threshold. There is no region switch for the simulator to stumble on, and the moderate-inversion region, where many low-power analog circuits operate, is described rather than patched over.

## The strong-inversion limit

For large positive $x$, $\ln(1 + e^x) \approx x$, so $F \approx x^2$. Substituting $x$ gives
$$I_D \approx I_{spec}\frac{(V_{GS} - V_t)^2}{(2n\,kT/q)^2},$$
which is the square law with an effective $k'/n$.

The approach is gradual. At overdrive 150 mV with $n = 1.5$, $x = 1.934$, $F = 4.282$ and $x^2 = 3.741$: the ratio is 1.14, still 14% above the square law. At 300 mV, $x = 3.87$ and the ratio falls to about 1.01.

That gradual approach is the moderate-inversion region, roughly a few $nkT/q$ either side of threshold, where neither asymptote is accurate. Piecewise models that switch from exponential to square law at a fixed point get this region wrong, which matters for $g_m/I_D$-based analog design and for near-threshold digital logic. Real models then add velocity saturation and mobility degradation on top of this core.

## The weak-inversion limit

For large negative $x$, $\ln(1 + e^x) \approx e^x$, so $F \approx e^{2x}$, and
$$I_D \approx I_{spec}\,e^{(V_{GS} - V_t)/(n\,kT/q)}.$$
This is the subthreshold exponential with swing $n(kT/q)\ln 10$.

Example: $n = 1.5$, overdrive -140 mV. $x = -1.805$, $F = 0.0232$ and $e^{2x} = 0.0270$; the ratio is 0.857. Deeper, at -300 mV, the ratio is about 0.98.

So one function covers both limits, with the transition placed by $V_t$ and its width set by $n\,kT/q$. For an extraction tool this structure is useful: subthreshold data constrain $n$ and $V_t$, strong-inversion data constrain $I_{spec}$ (mobility and $C_{ox}$), and the moderate region tests whether the interpolation is right. For a simulator developer it shows why compact models are smooth by construction rather than by careful patching of region boundaries.

## Going deeper

label: BSIM
lesson:
# BSIM

BSIM, the Berkeley Short-channel IGFET Model family, is the most widely used set of industry-standard MOSFET compact models. Its members cover planar bulk devices (BSIM4), silicon on insulator (BSIM-SOI), multi-gate FinFETs and gate-all-around devices (BSIM-CMG) and independent-gate FD-SOI (BSIM-IMG). Foundry PDKs ship BSIM model cards, standard-cell characterization runs SPICE with them, and every timing number a design sees passes through one.

## The BSIM family

BSIM models are developed at UC Berkeley and standardized through the Compact Model Coalition, which qualifies models and releases so that one foundry model file runs consistently across simulators.

BSIM3 and its successor BSIM4 model planar bulk MOSFETs. BSIM4 added effects that became important in deep submicron nodes, such as gate tunneling current, stress and layout-dependent effects, and more detailed parasitics.

BSIM-SOI models partially and fully depleted SOI, including the floating body node and self-heating.

BSIM-CMG (common multi-gate) models devices whose gates are tied together around the channel: FinFETs and, in later versions, gate-all-around nanosheets. Its instance parameters include fin count, fin height and fin thickness.

BSIM-IMG (independent multi-gate) models devices with separately biased front and back gates, such as ultra-thin-body FD-SOI with back biasing.

Picking the model is the first decision in any extraction or simulation flow: equations, parameters and instance geometry all depend on it.

## Inside a BSIM model card

BSIM4 is threshold-voltage based: it builds a threshold expression with short-channel, narrow-width and body-bias terms, then a unified current expression across regions with smoothing functions. BSIM-CMG is surface-potential based: it solves the electrostatics of the multi-gate body for the surface potential and derives charge and current from it, adding corrections for quantum confinement in thin bodies (a threshold shift and a charge-centroid offset).

A model card holds hundreds of parameters covering threshold, mobility and its degradation, velocity saturation, DIBL, output conductance, parasitic resistance and capacitance, leakage components, noise and temperature dependence. Only a subset is tuned for a given process.

Foundry cards often use binning: parameters are fitted separately over ranges of $W$ and $L$, each with size-dependent terms of the form $P = P_0 + P_L/L + P_W/W + P_P/(WL)$, and the simulator chooses the bin by instance geometry. Bin boundaries must be continuous, or a sizing optimizer that changes width across a boundary sees a jump.

## BSIM in tools

Reference BSIM releases are distributed as Verilog-A source as well as being implemented inside commercial simulators. A Verilog-A compiler path lets a simulator load the exact reference model, with derivatives generated automatically, instead of hand-porting the equations into C, where implementations can diverge.

In open source, ngspice includes BSIM3 and BSIM4 natively and can load compiled Verilog-A models, including BSIM-CMG, through its OSDI interface, with OpenVAF as one compiler that produces OSDI binaries. This combination is what lets open-source flows simulate FinFET PDKs.

In a PDK flow, the BSIM card drives standard-cell characterization: SPICE runs per cell, arc, input slew, output load and PVT corner build the Liberty timing and power tables that static timing and power analysis consume.

Model versions are pinned exactly. Parameters are extracted against one version's equations, and running them under another version can shift currents and charges, so PDKs specify both the model and its version.

## Going deeper

Chauhan and others, "FinFET Modeling for IC Simulation and Design: Using the BSIM-CMG Standard" (2015); the BSIM4 and BSIM-CMG technical manuals from the BSIM group; the ngspice manual, OSDI chapter.

# Compact-model parameter extraction

Parameter extraction fits a compact model's parameters to measured or TCAD-simulated device data. It starts with simple, physically motivated extractions of threshold and transconductance factor, then fits short-channel, mobility, parasitic and leakage terms region by region, and ends with a global least-squares polish. The procedure is well defined and checkable, which is why it is a natural task for an automated or agent-driven flow.

## Threshold by linear extrapolation

In the linear region at small $V_{DS}$, $I_D \approx k'(W/L)(V_{GS} - V_t - V_{DS}/2)V_{DS}$ is linear in $V_{GS}$. Real curves bend because of mobility degradation and series resistance, so the standard method takes the tangent at the point of maximum transconductance and extrapolates it to zero current:
$$V_t = V_{GS,0} - \frac{I_{D,0}}{g_{m,max}} - \frac{V_{DS}}{2},$$
where $V_{GS,0}$ and $I_{D,0}$ are the bias and current at maximum $g_m$.

Example: $V_{DS} = 50$ mV, maximum $g_m = 250$ µA/V at $V_{GS} = 0.7$ V where $I_D = 40$ µA. $V_t = 0.7 - 0.16 - 0.025 = 0.515$ V.

Other definitions are common: constant current (the $V_{GS}$ at which $I_D = I_0 \cdot W/L$, for a chosen $I_0$), and second-derivative peak. They give different numbers for the same device, so an extraction report must state its method, and comparing thresholds across sources requires the same definition.

## Threshold from saturation data

In saturation the long-channel law $I_D = \tfrac12 K(V_{GS} - V_t)^2$, with $K = k'W/L$, makes $\sqrt{I_D}$ linear in $V_{GS}$. Two points determine the line:
$$V_t = \frac{V_2\sqrt{I_1} - V_1\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2}}.$$

Example: $I_1 = 32$ µA at 0.8 V and $I_2 = 128$ µA at 1.2 V. $\sqrt{I_1} = 5.657$ and $\sqrt{I_2} = 11.314$, so $V_t = (1.2 \times 5.657 - 0.8 \times 11.314)/(5.657 - 11.314) = 0.4$ V.

In practice an extraction fits a line through many points rather than two, which is a linear least-squares problem, and checks the residuals. Curvature in $\sqrt{I_D}$ reveals velocity saturation and mobility degradation, which the square law ignores. That is why staged extraction uses long-channel devices for these first parameters: their behavior is closest to the simple law, so the fitted values are physical.

## The transconductance factor and staged fitting

The slope of $\sqrt{I_D}$ against $V_{GS}$ is $\sqrt{K/2}$, so
$$K = 2\left(\frac{\sqrt{I_2} - \sqrt{I_1}}{V_2 - V_1}\right)^2.$$
Example: the same points give slope $5.657/0.4 = 14.14$ and $K = 400$ µA/V$^2$.

Production extraction is staged. Long-wide devices fix threshold, body effect and low-field mobility. Short devices add roll-off, DIBL, velocity saturation and output conductance. Narrow devices add width effects. Then come parasitic resistance, capacitances from C-V data, leakage components and temperature coefficients. Each stage fits the parameters that dominate in a chosen bias and geometry region, holding earlier ones fixed, which keeps each fit well conditioned and the values physical.

A final global optimization, usually weighted least squares on log current for subthreshold data and relative error elsewhere, polishes everything together. Parameter bounds keep the optimizer from trading physical meaning for fit quality.

## Going deeper

Schroder, "Semiconductor Material and Device Characterization" (3rd ed.), chapter 4; Ortiz-Conde and others, "A review of recent MOSFET threshold voltage extraction methods", Microelectronics Reliability (2002).

label: Parameter extraction as a Tier 1 skill
lesson:
# Parameter extraction as a Tier 1 skill

Compact-model parameter extraction is a near-ideal agent task: the inputs are data, the outputs are parameter values, the model equations are fixed, and a simulator scores the result. In the four-layer engine view it is configuration, Tier 1. Packaging it as a skill with a manifest, golden tests and a clear boundary for when a request stops being a fit and becomes a code change is what makes it safe to automate.

## Which tier a modeling request lands in

Change tiers apply directly to device modeling.

Tier 1, configuration: new values in a model card, with model equations unchanged. Refitting BSIM-CMG parameters to new wafer data, retargeting a corner card, or adjusting temperature coefficients are all Tier 1. No recompile, and the most common request.

Tier 2, plug-in: a new behavior at a defined extension point, such as a threshold-shift term that depends on a layout-proximity quantity the model lacks, or a custom aging law. It is written as a model extension, for example a Verilog-A module or a compiled plug-in, and the simulator core is untouched.

Tier 3, core: a change to the simulator itself, such as Newton step limiting, matrix assembly or time-step control. It affects every circuit, needs human approval and full regression, and should be rare.

An agent fitting parameters that discovers the fit only works with a new equation must stop and escalate to the plug-in path, with its own tests, rather than quietly editing the model during a Tier 1 task.

## The extraction skill and its manifest

A skill packages the extraction engine with a plain-language manifest that an agent can read without opening the source. For extraction it should declare: the supported model and version (BSIM4 4.8, BSIM-CMG 110, and so on); the required measurements (I-V families, C-V, temperatures, geometries); which parameters it fits, in what stages, with what bounds; the tunables (stage weights, error metrics, bias ranges); and the fit report it returns.

Selection is a cheap text decision: match the device type and model version in a request against manifests. Running a planar extraction on FinFET data would fit the wrong equations, however low the error.

Good extraction skills fit in stages, threshold first, then mobility and short-channel terms, then parasitics, using the bias region where each parameter dominates, and expose bounds so that fits stay physical. These choices are exactly the tunables a manifest should advertise, since different processes need different ranges.

## Verifying and promoting extraction skills

Every extraction skill ships golden tests: a reference dataset whose fit must reproduce a known-good card and error report within tolerance. The harness reruns them on every edit to the skill.

A Tier 1 refit that lowers fit error still needs a differential check before promotion: benchmark circuits (ring oscillators, inverter chains, a few cells) simulated with the old and new cards must move only as intended. A better device fit can shift circuit behavior in a region nobody looked at.

Measured wafer data is customer IP. The skill runs on-site, inside a sandbox with no network, and only the reusable improvement (a better staging sequence, a better bound set) can leave as know-how. The customer's data and cards do not.

An improved sequence found for one tricky process goes through the flywheel: iterate as a plug-in, validate with golden and differential tests, then promote it into the shared skill library, where its manifest makes it selectable for future requests.

## Going deeper

The repository's docs/eda/agent-first-concepts.md, sections 2, 4 and 7; Schroder, "Semiconductor Material and Device Characterization" (3rd ed.), chapter 4, for the underlying extraction methods.

label: Compact-model plug-ins at the simulator seam
lesson:
# Compact-model plug-ins at the simulator seam

A circuit simulator's most important seam is the boundary between the solver and the device models. The solver's Newton loop, matrix assembly and time stepping are settled mathematics; device physics varies by technology and by customer. Placing a narrow, stable interface there lets new or customized models arrive as plug-ins, Tier 2 changes, without touching the core. Designing that seam well is a concrete exercise in the agent-first engine model.

## What crosses the seam

The solver asks one question per device evaluation: at these terminal voltages, temperature and instance parameters, what are the terminal currents, the terminal charges, and their derivatives with respect to the voltages? The answer fills the residual vector and the Jacobian. That is the whole interface.

The immutable core is matrix assembly, the Newton loop with its convergence checks, time-step control and the linear solver. The change surface is the device models: BSIM equations, a customer's self-heating variant, a process-specific stress term, a learned model.

Real models need internal nodes, for series resistance, a floating body or a thermal node, so the seam must let a model declare internal nodes and the equations for them. A seam that passes only terminal values would force self-heating into the core.

A working example exists in open source: OSDI, the binary interface through which ngspice loads compiled Verilog-A models. Verilog-A itself is the authoring language, and a compiler such as OpenVAF generates the evaluation code and derivatives.

## Rules that keep the seam fast and correct

Derivatives must be accurate and consistent with the currents. Finite-difference derivatives carry truncation and roundoff error that slows or breaks Newton convergence; compilers that generate analytic derivatives exist for this reason.

Calls should be coarse. Model evaluation is the hot loop of circuit simulation, and a virtual call per device with scattered data defeats vectorization. Evaluating many instances of one model type per call keeps overhead low and lets the model vectorize.

Plug-ins must be deterministic, with no hidden global state, so parallel evaluation gives the same result on every run regardless of thread scheduling.

A plug-in that passes its own unit tests has proved only its code. The harness must also run golden I-V and C-V sweeps and benchmark circuits through the real simulator, because what matters is behavior inside Newton across bias and temperature.

## Robustness, versioning and new model types

Newton iterations visit wild voltages before converging. A plug-in that returns NaN or overflows at $V_{GS} = -2$ V, a bias no normal test covers, will crash simulations unpredictably. The harness should sweep stress biases beyond the operating range and check for finite, bounded outputs and derivatives.

The extension ABI should be frozen and versioned. If it changes, existing plug-ins may break, so changing it is itself a core change with a migration cost.

The seam does not care how a model computes. A neural-network device model plugs in at the same place, but must meet the same contract: smooth currents and charges, consistent derivatives, charge conservation and sensible behavior outside its training data.

Agent-written plug-ins are iterated quickly, so they run in a sandbox with CPU, memory and time limits and no network, which contains failures and protects the IP boundary.

## Going deeper

The OSDI specification and OpenVAF documentation; the repository's docs/eda/agent-first-concepts.md, sections 1, 5 and 6; McAndrew and others, "Best practices for compact modeling in Verilog-A", IEEE Journal of the Electron Devices Society (2015).

problems.a: Models declaring internal nodes and their equations, so the solver adds unknowns
problems.e: Real models have internal nodes for series resistance, body or temperature. A seam that only passes terminal values would force self-heating into the core.

problems.e: The solver assembles the matrix. The model answers one question: what are this device's currents, charges and Jacobian entries at this bias.

label: Golden I-V tests for model changes
prereqs: Compact-model plug-ins at the simulator seam
lesson:
# Golden I-V tests for model changes

Every compact-model change, whether a refit, a plug-in edit or a new model version, must prove that it changed only what it was meant to change. Golden I-V tests compare the candidate against a frozen, trusted baseline at fixed bias points; differential tests check that the differences land only where intended. Designing the suite, choosing the error metric and tolerance, and reading the results are concrete verification skills for an agentic modeling loop.

## What a golden suite contains

A golden suite must exercise every output the simulator uses, in every region: $I_D$-$V_{GS}$ families at low and high drain bias (subthreshold, threshold, strong inversion), $I_D$-$V_{DS}$ families, C-V curves, derivatives such as $g_m$ and $g_{ds}$, and several temperatures and geometries. It should include the Gummel symmetry test around $V_{DS} = 0$, which catches asymmetric or non-smooth behavior that breaks analog and RF simulation.

The golden reference values come from the previously validated model version, run through the same simulator on fixed inputs. Generating them from the code under test would prove nothing.

Benchmark circuits complete the suite: ring oscillators, inverter chains and a few standard cells. They integrate current and charge over real transitions, so they catch changes that point tests miss.

A suite certifies only what it exercises. Coverage of temperature, geometry and bias is the first thing to review when a change passes tests but misbehaves later.

## Checking points against a tolerance

Compare each candidate current with its golden value by relative error,
$$e = \frac{|I_{cand} - I_{gold}|}{I_{gold}},$$
and fail any point with $e$ above the tolerance. Equivalently, compare $\log I$ for subthreshold points.

Example with a 1% tolerance: golden 120.0 µA, candidate 120.6 µA gives 0.5%, a pass. Golden 0.250 µA, candidate 0.254 µA gives 1.6%, a fail, though its absolute error, 4 nA, is far smaller than the first point's 600 nA.

Absolute error would ignore the subthreshold region entirely, since currents span many decades. A tolerance of exactly zero is also a poor choice: compiler and platform differences change the last bits of floating point, so tests would fail with no real change. Tolerances should be tight enough to catch meaningful shifts and loose enough to absorb roundoff, well below typical fitting error.

## Differential checks

A golden test says whether results changed; a differential test says whether they changed only where intended. For an edit that adds a gate-induced drain leakage term, the expected difference is confined to negative $V_{GS}$ at high $V_{DS}$; every other region should match the baseline within tolerance. A difference anywhere else is a bug, however good the new term looks.

Some failures hide from point tests. A change to the charge or capacitance model can pass every DC I-V point but shift a ring oscillator's frequency, because delay depends on charge as well as current. A change to a mobility temperature coefficient can pass a suite that covers only nominal temperature and corrupt hot and cold corners.

The same structure applies at library level: a differential characterization of a few cells, comparing delay and power tables before and after, shows whether a model change propagates to timing as expected. Only after golden and differential checks pass is a change shown to a human as a reviewable diff.

## Going deeper

The repository's docs/eda/agent-first-concepts.md, section 6; McAndrew, "Validation of MOSFET model source-drain symmetry", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (2006).

label: ML surrogates for TCAD in DTCO loops
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# ML surrogates for TCAD in DTCO loops

Design-technology co-optimization explores many device options, but each 3D TCAD point is slow. A machine-learned surrogate trained on TCAD runs can predict device characteristics in milliseconds, which turns exploration into a fast inner loop. The surrogate is a fast engine; TCAD remains the accurate one. Deciding when to trust the surrogate and when to recurse to TCAD is the core of using it well.

## Surrogates as the fast engine

A TCAD surrogate learns a map from device design inputs, such as gate length, fin or sheet dimensions, spacer thickness and doping, to outputs such as I-V curves on a fixed bias grid, threshold, swing, DIBL, capacitances or compact-model parameters. Training data comes from TCAD runs over a designed set of inputs.

The value is speed. If a TCAD point takes minutes to hours and a surrogate takes milliseconds, a DTCO loop can sweep thousands of options, run optimizers and study variability, then re-simulate only the promising candidates in TCAD before decisions are made. This is the fast-versus-accurate engine pattern: the fast engine explores, the accurate engine confirms.

Output representation matters for integration. A surrogate that emits compact-model parameters or I-V curves on the grid that extraction already consumes drops into existing flows; one that emits raw mesh values or a pass-fail flag does not.

## When to recurse to TCAD

Optimizers seek the corners of a model. If a DTCO optimizer drives the surrogate to a geometry outside its training range and reports a record drive current, that result is untrusted extrapolation. The loop must re-simulate the point in TCAD before believing it, and the confirmed point can be added to the training set.

A surrogate should therefore report uncertainty, for example from an ensemble of models, and flag inputs far from its training data. High uncertainty is the trigger to recurse; this is also how active learning chooses where to spend new TCAD runs.

A surrogate is only as current as its training data. When the TCAD deck is recalibrated to new silicon, the surrogate is stale and must be checked against new runs and retrained; versioning the surrogate with the deck it learned keeps this visible.

Validation should match the decision: error on held-out TCAD runs in the region the decision depends on, and agreement with TCAD on the ranking of candidates, since a decision depends on ordering.

## Physics, rewards and sampling

A surrogate that sometimes predicts current falling as gate voltage rises violates physics and breaks downstream solvers and extraction. Constraints such as monotonicity in $V_{GS}$, positivity and smoothness should be built into the surrogate's form or training loss, or the surrogate should predict quantities from which a physical model is constructed.

When a reinforcement-learning agent or optimizer uses the surrogate as its reward, it will exploit surrogate errors: reward hacking. The reward rises while true TCAD performance does not. Periodic TCAD scoring of the best candidates keeps the reward honest.

The surrogate inherits every error of the TCAD deck, so its accuracy is bounded by how well that deck is calibrated to silicon. It approximates TCAD, not reality.

With a fixed TCAD budget, training data should first cover the input space with a space-filling design, to avoid blind spots, and then concentrate near decision boundaries or optima through active learning, where accuracy pays.

## Going deeper

The repository's docs/eda/agent-first-concepts.md, sections 8 and 9; Forrester, Sóbester and Keane, "Engineering Design via Surrogate Modelling" (2008).

problems.a: Each 3D TCAD point can take minutes to hours, while a trained surrogate evaluates in milliseconds
problems.e: The speed gap enables sweeps, optimization and uncertainty studies that would be unaffordable with TCAD alone.

label: Tool-grounded rewards for model fitting
prereqs: Parameter extraction as a Tier 1 skill
lesson:
# Tool-grounded rewards for model fitting

When an agent or a reinforcement-learning loop fits compact-model parameters, its reward should come from tools, not opinions: simulate the candidate card and score it against measurements and physical constraints. Designing that tool-grounded reward is where device knowledge matters. The error metric must weight every region, the reward must check behavior beyond the fitted points, and the agent must not be able to improve the score by changing the reference.

## Designing the reward

A tool-grounded extraction reward is computed by simulating the candidate card and comparing it with measured (or TCAD) data. It should include several parts.

Error across all regions, measured in a way that respects decades of current: log error in subthreshold, relative error elsewhere.

Errors in derivatives such as $g_m$ and $g_{ds}$, since a fit can match currents while getting slopes wrong, which ruins analog gain, delay and Newton behavior.

Penalties for nonphysical parameters and broken smoothness, such as parameters outside physical bounds, non-monotone currents or discontinuous derivatives.

Generalization: some geometries held out of the fit and scored separately, since a card must predict every legal width and length.

Fast proxies, such as error at a handful of bias points, are tempting because they are cheap. But a proxy can be optimized while full-curve or circuit behavior gets worse, so the full evaluation must run periodically to close the gap.

## Root-mean-square log error

A common core metric is the RMS of the base-ten log ratio between model and measurement over $N$ points:
$$E = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\log_{10}\frac{I_{model,i}}{I_{meas,i}}\right]^2},$$
with reward $-E$ or a decreasing function of it.

Example: ratios 1.1, 0.9 and 2.0. The logs are 0.0414, -0.0458 and 0.3010; their squares average to 0.0314, and $E = 0.177$.

Log error treats a factor of 2 high and a factor of 2 low equally, and treats a 10% error at 1 mA and at 10 pA equally, which is what subthreshold-sensitive applications need. Squaring makes large errors dominate, so one badly fitted point can outweigh many good ones; a maximum-error term or robust loss can be added when worst-case behavior matters. The metric is only as good as the points it is computed on, which brings coverage back to the center.

## How the reward gets gamed

Reward hacking in extraction takes recognizable forms.

Compensating parameters: a near-perfect score with a parameter pinned at its bound often means the model is absorbing a missing effect into the wrong knob. The card may extrapolate badly; check physical plausibility and held-out behavior.

Unscored regions: if data stops at $V_{DS} = 0.8$ V, a card whose current falls with $V_{DS}$ above 0.9 V costs nothing. Physical sanity checks over the whole qualified range, such as monotonicity and positive output conductance, belong in the reward.

Altering the reference: an agent that smooths or trims measured data before fitting lowers error by changing the ground truth. The reward's inputs must be immutable to the agent.

Device-level averages: low average error can hide errors exactly where circuits operate. Including a circuit benchmark, such as ring-oscillator delay or a cell's delay table, scores what the card is for.

Each guard is cheap compared with shipping a card that silently mispredicts a corner.

problems.q:
Why should an extraction reward include errors in $g_m$ and $g_{ds}$, not only in $I_D$?

A) Derivatives are not used by simulators

B) A fit can match currents while getting their slopes wrong, which ruins gain, delay and Newton behaviour

C) Including them makes the reward easier to game

D) Derivatives are always correct when currents are
problems.a: A fit can match currents while getting their slopes wrong, which ruins gain, delay and Newton behaviour
problems.e: Analog gain depends on $g_m/g_{ds}$, and the solver needs consistent derivatives. Currents alone under-constrain the fit.

problems.q:
Why are fast proxies dangerous as rewards in extraction?

A) Rewards cannot be computed quickly

B) Fast proxies are always exact

C) Proxies make the simulator slower

D) A proxy, such as error at a few bias points, can be optimized while the full-curve or circuit behaviour gets worse
problems.a: A proxy, such as error at a few bias points, can be optimized while the full-curve or circuit behaviour gets worse
problems.e: This is reward hacking: the agent improves the measured number, not the goal. Periodic scoring with the full evaluation closes the gap.

problems.q:
Measured data comes from five device geometries. How should the reward be validated?

A) Skip validation when training error is low

B) Use a different technology for validation

C) Score only the devices used for fitting

D) Hold out some geometries, fit on the rest and score the held-out ones, so scalability is tested
problems.a: Hold out some geometries, fit on the rest and score the held-out ones, so scalability is tested
problems.e: A card must predict every legal W and L. Holding out geometries tests generalization, the way held-out data does for any model.

problems.q:
A fitting reward scores a compact-model candidate by the RMS of $\log_{10}(I_{model}/I_{meas})$ over the measured points. The ratios $I_{model}/I_{meas}$ at 3 points are 1.25, 1.5, 3. What is the RMS log error?

A) 0.250

B) 0.477

C) 0.299

D) 0.089

E) 1.199
problems.e: Take $\log_{10}$ of each ratio, square, average over 3 points and take the square root: 0.299. Log error treats a factor of 2 high and a factor of 2 low equally, at any current level.

problems.q:
An agent's fit scores a near-perfect reward but one mobility parameter sits at its lower bound. What should a reviewer suspect?

A) The measurement data is perfect

B) The fit is certainly correct

C) The parameter is compensating for a missing effect, and the card may extrapolate badly

D) The bound has no effect on the fit
problems.a: The parameter is compensating for a missing effect, and the card may extrapolate badly
problems.e: Parameters pinned at bounds often signal that the model is absorbing an effect into the wrong knob. Check physical plausibility and held-out behaviour.

problems.q:
A reward uses only data up to $V_{DS} = 0.8$ V. The agent finds a card that fits perfectly but whose current falls with $V_{DS}$ above 0.9 V. Why was this not penalized?

A) Currents always fall above 0.9 V

B) The simulator rejected the card

C) The reward never evaluated that region, so a non-monotone extrapolation was free

D) The reward penalized it automatically
problems.a: The reward never evaluated that region, so a non-monotone extrapolation was free
problems.e: Add physical sanity checks over the full qualified range, such as monotonicity and positive output conductance, to the reward.
